item.title: Sister June Carpenter, the Oldest Shaker, Has Died
item.description:
Sister June Carpenter, a gentle librarian and one of three practicing members of the last active Shaker group in America, a Christian community of celibate pacifists, died on Nov. 3. She was 88.

Her death was announced by her community in a social media post that said she had been struggling with health and mobility issues, but did not provide further details.

At Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village in New Gloucester, Maine, there are 18 lovely brick and clapboard buildings bounded roadside by a white picket fence, set on a lake and 1,800 acres of farmland, woods and wetlands. But there aren’t legions of Shakers in residence.

At this point, there are only two: Brother Arnold Hadd, 70, and Sister April Baxter, who joined last year and is around 60.

Reports of the group’s extinction are a constant source of irritation to them. The oft-used newspaper headline, “The Last Shaker This or That,” particularly grates.

Most inquiries from the news media are politely declined because of reporters’ tendency to focus on the dwindling population. In one instance, media coverage may have exacerbated the situation. In 2006, after The Boston Globe published a story about the community headlined “The Last Man Standing,” one of its members, Brother Wayne Smith, fell in love with the reporter and left.

Yet the public is welcome; one never knows who might be a prospective convert.

The Shaker ideology of pacifism, celibacy and communal living — and of a loving God who embraces both genders, or a Mother-Father spirit, as it is called — beckons many these days. Would-be novices are not uncommon. As Stacey Chase, the Boston Globe reporter, noted in her story, the village can receive as many as 70 inquiries a year. But not many applicants can commit.

Perhaps that is why Sabbathday Lake has such a robust community of Shaker-adjacents and friends: paid workers and volunteers who maintain the museum, help with the farm work — there are some 200 sheep and a few cows — tend to the herb garden and its harvest, offer workshops and preside over the sales of packaged herbs, teas, yarn, furniture, candles and other goodies in the gift shop and online store. Sunday services at the Meeting House are open to all, not just the members.

A bit of history: The Shakers landed in North America in 1774 after fleeing England, where they had been persecuted for their separatist beliefs — notably their opposition to the hierarchy of the Anglican Church — and their concept of a dual-gendered God. They earned a reputation as the Shaking Quakers because of the ecstatic movements they practiced in their worship. It was a slur, but the name stuck. Those swirling dances went out of favor decades ago, though Shakers still clap and stomp a bit, as various hymns require, during the Sunday meeting.

The Sabbathday Lake community, established in 1783, was one of 11 Shaker orders in the U.S. The numbers soon swelled to 15, with some 5,000 members spread between them. In the mid-19th century, the Sabbathday Lake family, like other Shaker communities, adopted a spiritual name for itself, Chosen Land. At the time, as Jeannine Lauber wrote in “Chosen Faith, Chosen Land: The Untold Story of America’s 21st-Century Shakers” (2009), it was the smallest and poorest of all the communities. Yet it outlasted them all.

When Ms. Carpenter first visited the village in the summer of 1988, she was 49; a friend took her to the dedication of its new library. In college, she had been drawn to stories of people who had religious vocations, and she felt that she, too, wanted to give her life to God. When she learned that the community needed help cataloging its archive for the new library, she volunteered to help, and felt so at home that she asked to be considered for membership.

After Sabbathday Lake’s head curator, David Richards, interviewed her, he declared, “If the meek are to inherit the earth, she will get the whole thing!”

Sister June may have been shy, but she had a quiet, arch sense of humor and, as the announcement of her death noted, a vast knowledge of the British royal family. In addition to working as a librarian, she tended the gardens and assisted in the kitchen.

Jere DeWaters, a retired professor of photography at the University of Maine at Augusta, spent eight years at Sabbathday Lake, starting in 1986, documenting the family. He recalled Sister June’s work at the renovated library — once the village’s schoolhouse — cataloging its extensive collection of manuscripts, photographs, journals and other written material that is a treasure trove for scholars.

“She was naturally shy, but had a wonderful smile when she looked up at the camera,” Mr. DeWaters said. “Not an outgoing person at all, but she did not miss a beat. One of the quiet ones, I think the old saying goes.”

As Sister June told Ms. Lauber, “I am the last and the least of the community at the moment, and I’m very happy in that position. If I get into a position where I’m head of something, like when I was head cataloger at the library where I used to work, I feel uncomfortable and insecure. But I can cope with being little and low. It helps with the humility that we are striving for.”

The Shakers are known for their faith, their furniture and their vast hymnody: “Simple Gifts,” often referred to by its opening line, “’Tis a gift to be simple,” is one of the best-known Shaker hymns. Sister June said she related most to another one:

Great I, little i, Great I can see.

Little i is pretty i, so little I will be.

June Carpenter was born on June 15, 1938, in Boston, the only child of Florence (Blanchard) Carpenter and Sydney Carpenter, a lawyer in private practice who went on to serve in the State Legislature.

She grew up in Brookline, in a religious family. They were regulars at the Federated Church, which combines a number of Protestant denominations, including American Baptist and Congregationalist.

One day, on a trip to Boston, she recalled having a spiritual awakening as she observed the crowds. “I could see that God was within each of them,” she told Ms. Lauber. “I’ve always remembered that — that God must be inside everyone in some way, whether they realize it or not.”

The feeling faded, she said, but the insight did not: “You can’t stay on the mountaintop forever. Like the Shakers say, ‘You have to come down into the valley,’ that’s where most of life is.”

After studying library science at Simmons College (now Simmons University) in Boston, she earned a master’s degree in 1964 and then went to work as a librarian for the Brookline Public Library.

Her father had died when she was 15, and she lived with her mother until her mother’s death in 1985.

Shakers are buried without individual markers, though fellow members note the deaths in the journals they keep of their daily lives. The cemetery at Sabbathday Lake has just one gravestone. It reads simply, “Shakers.”

Sister June, with typical modesty, requested no funeral service or visiting hours.

item.title: With Huang Out, Asian Americans Lose a Star, and Fear What Comes Next
item.description:
Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia has prompted fears about its plunging stock, China’s espionage efforts and the future of America’s A.I. competitiveness.

But for some Asian Americans, especially those of Chinese and Taiwanese descent working in technology, the rapid downfall of the powerful C.E.O. has come with another layer of disappointment, as well as fear.

To many, Mr. Huang was a hero — one of the few who smashed through the bamboo ceiling that has long stymied many Asian and Asian American professionals from reaching the C-suite, and did so with an energy that defied stereotypes of Asian Americans as timid or complacent in the workplace.

“He had a swagger,” said Dave Lu, managing partner of Hyphen Capital and a Taiwanese American veteran of Silicon Valley. “To see that exemplified was very inspirational.”

Mr. Lu said that he had been fielding messages from Asian and Asian American tech executives ever since The New York Times reported that Mr. Huang, the Taiwanese American chief executive of Nvidia, had an extramarital affair with a woman that U.S. intelligence services believe to be a Chinese spy.

Nvidia’s board has opened an investigation into his conduct, and Mr. Huang resigned from the company on Thursday. President Trump said Monday that Mr. Huang told him that he was unaware that the woman was an intelligence operative for Beijing.

“I think people feel severely disappointed and let down,” Mr. Lu said. “We thought he was infallible and invincible because he seemed like a superhero.”

In interviews, many Asian Americans agreed that Mr. Huang had demonstrated poor judgment and should be held accountable. The Times has also reported that Mr. Huang had another extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who was his direct subordinate.

“If I were on the board, I would fire him,” said Buck Gee, the Northern California regional chair for the Committee of 100, a Chinese American advocacy group, who has been outspoken about the relative lack of Asian Americans in higher management.

But there is also growing unease about how Asians in America may be affected by the fallout.

Some said that social media memes about Mr. Huang and Alice Huang, the executive who the U.S. identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, had reinforced harmful stereotypes about Asian immigrants and their descendants as having divided loyalties, or Asian women as hypersexualized honey traps.

“There is so much suspicion of Chinese Americans as spies, traitors, thieves of trade secrets, agents of influence, the last thing we need is another individual of Chinese background implicated in these issues,” said Frank H. Wu, author of “Yellow: Race in America Beyond Black and White.”

There are also concerns that such stereotypes can feed into government overreach.

Many still remember the China Initiative, a Justice Department program that began under the first Trump administration and was intended to fight Chinese economic espionage. Critics said the program singled out scientists based on their ethnicity and blurred the line between violations of disclosure policies and more serious crimes like espionage. Many of the prosecutions against academics of Chinese descent eventually collapsed, and the initiative was ultimately shuttered by the Biden administration.

“Certainly there’s fear in the Asian American and the scientific community that once again we’ll be scapegoated as national security risks,” said John C. Yang, president of Asian Americans Advancing Justice, a civil rights organization.

The disappointment for some Asian Americans stems from the pride that they took in Mr. Huang’s story.

While Mr. Huang was not the only prominent American tech executive of East Asian descent, his immigrant journey from Taiwan was well known.

Born in Taiwan to a chemical engineer father and a schoolteacher mother, Mr. Huang spent some time in Thailand before moving to the United States. In interviews, he has talked about the racist taunts he faced as a child while attending a religious reform school in Kentucky.

Mr. Huang went on to receive a degree in electrical engineering from Oregon State University, and then a master’s degree from Stanford University. Then, in 1993, at the age of 30, he co-founded Nvidia with two friends in a booth at Denny’s — the same chain where he once worked as a teenager busing tables.

As chief executive, Mr. Huang went on to build Nvidia into a company worth $5.7 trillion at its peak and a dominant force in artificial intelligence. Along the way, he also cultivated a rock star persona. President Trump was a big fan, Mr. Huang was often mobbed by admirers in Taiwan and China, and his leather jackets became iconic.

“He was the most recognizable East Asian American C.E.O.,” said Elaine Chen, who works to push Asian American leadership in the private sector.

To many Asian Americans, his rise was even more impressive given the challenges that they had long faced in Silicon Valley. While Asians account for about half of the Silicon Valley work force, they make up only 25 percent or so of executives, said Mr. Gee, citing his analysis of recent data released by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.

Experts attribute the discrepancy in part to the model minority stereotype, which they say has contributed to a view of Asian Americans as smart but lacking the assertiveness needed to be successful business leaders.

“Jensen Huang represented an ideal type who shattered the bamboo ceiling: visionary, creative, innovative, bold, charismatic, and assertive without being brash,” said Jennifer Lee, a professor at Columbia University who has written extensively about the challenges that Asian Americans face in the workplace.

Others were more worried that the targeting of Mr. Huang could be an ominous sign that China was becoming bolder in its efforts to influence the diaspora.

“I have no doubt that there’s a lot of spying going on in Silicon Valley,” Mr. Gee said. “Everyone knows that.”

item.title: Trump Signals New Strategy on Iran: A Waiting Game
item.description:
President Trump says he is leaning toward a new solution to the Iran nuclear crisis: Declare it is over, even if not much has changed.

Mr. Trump and his team have taken to asserting that they have the Iranians right where they want them. They say they no longer need a new nuclear agreement that would remove potential bomb fuel from the country, or to limit Iran’s missile capability, two of the leading reasons the president cited 10 months ago for going to war.

Mr. Trump appears — at least for now — to have rejected a series of military options that would involve intense, if time-limited, attacks on military installations, nuclear sites and even some energy infrastructure.

All the talk this year of sending in commandos to seize roughly 970 pounds of uranium from the country, enriched to a near-bomb-grade level of 60 percent purity, has been abandoned, albeit for the moment. So has the detailed analysis of whether America’s biggest bunker busters are powerful enough to get deep into Pickaxe Mountain, a site U.S. intelligence believes — but is not sure — is the location of advanced centrifuges that can purify uranium into bomb fuel.

In comments to reporters this week in Paris, where he was attending a meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of 7, Secretary of State Marco Rubio described an approach best characterized as strategic patience: waiting for sanctions on Iran to take their toll and ultimately crack their government.

“At this point, the economic campaign and the pressure and the devastation that our economic campaign is having on the Iranian regime is working so well that the president really doesn’t have any need to conduct major combat operations,” Mr. Rubio said.

If Iran “crosses certain red lines” the United States could intervene, he added, because it has “the most capable military in the world.”

The new approach was underscored on Thursday when Mr. Trump announced that he was redirecting Vice President JD Vance away from his efforts to engage in direct negotiations with Iran’s top security official, Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council and a former commander in chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

The vice president, who has blamed the war for the widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections, had previously positioned himself to play a key role in bringing the conflict to a negotiated end.

Now Mr. Trump seems to think that a negotiation would be a waste of Mr. Vance’s time. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Mr. Trump wrote in a social media post. “Those days have long since passed.” He said it was more important for Mr. Vance to investigate cities and states run by Democrats, and to hunt down wasted federal funds.

Meanwhile, he asserted that he had all the leverage over Iran he needed. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars,” he wrote, overstating the amount of Iranian assets held by the United States and its allies, “and we’ve got their Strait!” (While estimates differ widely, there may be upward of $100 billion of Iranian funds frozen in various accounts around the world, but only $2 billion or so in the United States.)

The Strait of Hormuz, which Iran disrupted within days of the initial attack, catching the United States flat-footed, has only partially reopened. Each day is a game of cat and mouse as the U.S. Navy tries to guide oil tankers out of the strait.

Despite Mr. Trump’s claims, there are no signs that the United States is packing up and going away. The naval blockade that has prevented Iran from shipping oil remains, officials say, and there is no immediate plan to end it. That suggests a continued, large-scale military presence in the region — exactly what Mr. Trump and his allies said in the spring they wanted to avoid.

Mr. Trump’s hope seems to be that with time, Iran will seep off the front pages as a major issue, and the regime, under greater and greater economic pressure, will crack. But it may not be that simple.

“The president may be finished with Iran, but Iran isn’t finished with him,” Suzanne Maloney, an Iran expert at the Brookings Institution, said on Friday. While the Navy now has oil shipments coming out of the Persian Gulf “near prewar levels,” she noted, it comes “at high cost and considerable uncertainty about its sustainability.”

Tehran will continue to disrupt transit through the strait, rebuild its missile and drone stockpiles, and reconstitute its nuclear program. And as Iran’s economic conditions deteriorate, its leadership is likely to escalate in an effort to relieve the pressure. So the United States remains mired in a stalemate in the Gulf that is likely to intensify rather than fade away.

And there is the nagging issue of that 60 percent enriched uranium. The near-bomb-grade fuel was the No. 1 reason Mr. Trump cited when he ordered the beginning of American attacks on Iran on Feb. 28. Now he sounds unconcerned about the stockpile.

“They have nothing,” Mr. Trump said on “60 Minutes” on Sunday, when Ross Douthat pressed him about the fuel. “It’s buried under thousands of tons of rock,” he said, noting that American spy satellites are watching it.

Of course, it has been sitting under that pile of rock since June 2025, when American bombers first struck three major Iranian nuclear sites: Fordo, Natanz and Isfahan.

At the time, the president said Iran’s nuclear capacity had been “obliterated.” It was an overstatement, experts said — the material was still there, intelligence reports assessed, but the attack certainly made it hard to retrieve.

While the fuel remains exactly where it was, apparently untouched, Mr. Trump’s arguments about it have shifted to match his current needs. He has said he ordered the strike in 2025 because Iran was “two weeks from being able to make a bomb.” It was not; if the fuel had been recovered, it might be two weeks away from having that uranium boosted to bomb-grade material. Fashioning it into a warhead would have taken months or years more.

Now he says it is nothing to worry about. But Mr. Trump’s latest declaration raises the central question: If the nuclear material is not a threat, sitting exactly where it was in February, why did America go to war?

“Trump began the war thinking he would be a hero,” said Karim Sadjadpour, an Iran expert at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. “He’s now trying to figure out how to end the war without looking like a loser.”

“He started with maximalist goals: ending Iran’s nuclear program, its missile production, its regional proxies and potentially the regime itself,” Mr. Sadjadpour added. “He now seems to be preparing for a minimalist outcome: accepting that the nuclear material is still there, as long as it’s buried under rock.”

Should Mr. Trump decide to give up and go home, he would presumably leave it to the Gulf allies, and perhaps the Europeans, to deal with what is left behind. The worry of many officials in the region is that Iran, to forestall a future attack, will decide it should find a way to produce a nuclear weapon — exactly the outcome Mr. Trump said he was determined to prevent.

item.title: Jeffries Leaves Nothing to Chance in Push to Lock Down Speakership
item.description:
Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, is pressing to wrap up his nomination to be speaker next week quickly and overwhelmingly, leaving potential detractors little room to maneuver around him even as some of them complain about an undemocratic process.

His allies this week began asking Democrats to sign a letter publicly signaling their backing for Mr. Jeffries ahead of the House Democrats’ closed-door leadership elections on Wednesday. Some of them think he deserves to be elected unanimously during that session, bypassing a vote by secret ballot that would give any dissenters a chance to register opposition. It would be a show of overwhelming unity and support, although Mr. Jeffries has not yet indicated whether he is seeking it.

But his allies are soliciting group endorsements to lock in backing from large factions, effectively shutting down any conversation about other options in an implicit sign that his nomination is inevitable. The New Democrat Coalition, a group of 114 center-left House Democrats and at least 40 members-elect, issued one such statement in support of Mr. Jeffries this week.

Mr. Jeffries has been meeting privately both with incumbents and new members to make his case, although he has yet to reach out to every newly elected member of the House. He is set next week to attend the Congressional Progressive Caucus board meeting, according to two people familiar with the plans, and his goal is to be in direct contact with every member by Wednesday.

The quiet campaign comes as Mr. Jeffries, in line to be the first Black speaker after presiding over sweeping Democratic victories and winning a historic majority, is facing some resistance from an energized left clamoring for a new face at the helm of the party for the new Congress. No one has stepped forward to challenge him.

But several Democrats elected last week would not commit during their campaigns to backing Mr. Jeffries for speaker. And many members are receiving an influx of calls and emails from progressives who say they are fed up with the Democratic Party establishment and see the leader, a reserved moderate, as an avatar of the status quo who is beholden to corporate interests.

Mr. Jeffries has publicly shrugged off the dissent — “You think I don’t have the votes nailed down?” he told a reporter this week, flashing a smile — but said that he takes “nothing for granted” and that part of the process was laying out “our vision for the future.”

At the same time, his allies are privately working to ensure any lingering resistance to Mr. Jeffries cannot derail him.

“There is an accurate sense of confidence that the votes are overwhelmingly there, but there’s an active whip operation underway to take no chances,” said Representative Jared Huffman, a progressive California Democrat who is part of Mr. Jeffries’s whip operation. He and other supporters of the leader are reaching out to each other and to other Democrats and “making sure this thing is airtight,” he added.

The push has alienated some incoming members who are openly chafing at what they view as an unfair process meant to engineer a predetermined outcome.

Representative-elect Don Leonard of Ohio has said he wants votes on ending U.S. aid to Israel and a constitutional amendment to overturn the Citizens United ruling that struck down limits on spending in politics. He said his first hours in Washington were an introduction to the hardball tactics.

In a video he posted online, Mr. Leonard said that unnamed “senior House Democrats” had threatened to make his life a “living hell” if he did not support Mr. Jeffries for speaker.

“We kind of knew this stuff was coming,” Mr. Leonard said in his video. “It’s a whole other thing when it’s in person, by people who actually care about you and are cheering for you but expect you to wear the team jersey and be a team player.” He later said that he had spoken with Mr. Jeffries and had expressed his concerns to him privately.

Some of Mr. Jeffries’s allies said that if new members wanted to kick off their congressional careers by opposing the first Black speaker, that was their prerogative but it would make little difference.

“Hakeem deserves it to be by acclamation,” said Representative Josh Gottheimer, Democrat of New Jersey, referring to a unanimous voice vote. “That said, if winning in places we’ve never won before and having a historic majority isn’t good enough for a few of our members, then let them vote ‘no.’”

Mr. Jeffries’s top lieutenants helping to shore up the vote said that despite some squeaky wheels, overall the process is lacking in real drama.

“I’ve been in a lot of whip organizations,” Representative Joseph D. Morelle, the New York Democrat overseeing new member orientation, said in an interview. “This is by far the easiest.”

Mr. Morelle said he had spoken to almost all of the new members and asked whether they had any concerns they wanted him to share with Mr. Jeffries. So far, he said, nobody had told him they planned to stand in the way.

That has not stopped some progressives from seeking to use the moment to press their agenda with Mr. Jeffries. Representative Pramila Jayapal, Democrat of Washington and a former chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said she was angling for a promise of a committee markup next year on a Medicare for All bill.

Ms. Jayapal conceded that with no one challenging Mr. Jeffries, her leverage to secure any concessions from him is minimal, but she argued he had plenty of incentives to embrace the liberal agenda.

“I’ve been explaining to people, you can’t beat somebody with nobody,” she said. “He knows he needs us, and we can be the wind behind his sails.” She would not say whether she would support Mr. Jeffries if he did not give her what she asked for.

“I’d like to believe we’re going to get a ‘yes,’” she said.

That’s an impression Mr. Jeffries has been leaving with other progressives, who said he appeared to be approaching conversations with an open mind.

Representative Delia Ramirez, Democrat of Illinois, told Drop Site News that she had met with Mr. Jeffries about bringing to the floor the Block the Bombs Act, which would withhold certain offensive weapons from Israel. She said that he did not give her a “no.”

Mr. Jeffries’s political challenge is the inverse of the one faced by his predecessor, Representative Nancy Pelosi, when she was working to round up the votes to be elected speaker in 2018. Back then, it was moderate Democrats who did not want to elevate the liberal congresswoman from San Francisco.

This time around, it is the progressives who are raising concerns. Mr. Jeffries has been steadfast in the face of criticism.

“Our track record of success, decisiveness and a historic victory over MAGA extremism speaks for itself,” Mr. Jeffries said in an interview last week. “There’s nothing else for anybody to say when it comes to what this House Democratic leadership team has been able to accomplish.”

Mr. Huffman, himself a senior member of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said the sniping from the left has been mostly noise.

“For now, there’s this little tempest,” he said. “I will wager that you’re going to see a surprisingly small number of protest votes.”

Even the new members who have complained that they are being steamrolled have not gone so far as to say they will not vote for Mr. Jeffries.

“It has been disappointing how undemocratic this process has felt,” Representative-elect Melat Kiros, a democratic socialist from Colorado who defeated an incumbent in the primary, told CNN. “I fiercely believe in the importance of competitive elections. It feels like a lot of our class are just coming in and being told: ‘This is what the leadership is going to be.’ ”

item.title: Former Oklahoma Death Row Prisoner Pleads Guilty to Lesser Charge
item.description:
Richard Glossip, who spent nearly 30 years on death row in Oklahoma before receiving a stay of execution from the U.S. Supreme Court, pleaded guilty to a lesser charge on Thursday in order to avoid a new murder trial.

Mr. Glossip, 63, pleaded guilty to accessory to murder after the fact, his lawyer, Don Knight, said in a statement. The plea agreement means that Mr. Glossip will not be retried on a first-degree murder charge.

Mr. Knight, a lawyer who specializes in death penalty cases, said he was seeking to have Mr. Glossip freed from prison for time served, but Oklahoma said it would pursue the maximum sentence of 45 years. A jury convicted Mr. Glossip of arranging the killing in 1997 of Barry Van Treese, a motel owner in Oklahoma City. Mr. Glossip has maintained his innocence for decades, and two independent investigations found errors involving both testimony and evidence in the case. He had been in prison for nearly 30 years before he was released in May.

“We believe Rich has more than paid his debt to society by spending nearly 30 years on death row, during which time he was served three last meals, and came within minutes of being executed for a crime he did not commit,” Mr. Knight said in a statement.

“In 1997, had Rich been given the longest possible sentence for the crime he pleaded guilty to today, he would never have been on death row and would have been released 10 years ago.”

The Supreme Court ordered a retrial last year after the state’s attorney general, Gentner Drummond, a Republican, made the rare request that the justices to throw out Mr. Glossip’s conviction. The state of Oklahoma had set execution dates for Mr. Glossip nine times before the retrial was ordered.

By pleading guilty, Mr. Drummond said on Thursday, Mr. Glossip “took some measure of responsibility for the murder of Barry Van Treese.”

The plea deal was “a difficult decision for me and, more importantly, the Van Treese family,” Mr. Drummond said. “We both recognize that this path ensures a conviction related to Mr. Van Treese’s murder and gives us the best chance to secure additional prison time for Glossip.”

Sentencing on the accessory charge is scheduled for Dec. 17 and 18. Mr. Knight told reporters on Thursday afternoon that he hoped Judge Natalie Mai would sentence Mr. Glossip to time served.

Mr. Glossip’s bid to avoid execution drew the support of Oklahoma lawmakers of both parties, and attention from celebrities like Kim Kardashian. Mr. Drummond himself has said that carrying out the death sentence would be a “grave injustice.”

At the time of his conviction in 1998, prosecutors argued that Mr. Glossip, who managed Mr. Van Treese’s motel, had promised the motel handyman, Justin Sneed, $10,000 to kill Mr. Van Treese.

Mr. Sneed beat Mr. Van Treese to death and pleaded guilty to first-degree murder. He received a life sentence in exchange for agreeing to testify against Mr. Glossip.

Mr. Glossip’s lawyers argued that Mr. Sneed had planned and carried out the killing on his own.

item.title: Lauren Boebert, a MAGA Favorite, Loses Her Re-election Bid in Colorado
item.description:
Representative Lauren Boebert, a hard-line Republican, on Friday narrowly lost her bid for re-election in a conservative Colorado district, according to The Associated Press, an outcome that showed just how deeply Democrats encroached into Republican territory this year.

Ms. Boebert, a fiery favorite of the MAGA movement, switched congressional districts a few years ago after her old seat in Colorado grew more competitive. But the change was not enough to keep her from being ousted by Eileen Laubacher, a Democrat and a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Ms. Laubacher declared victory on Monday, and was leading by more than 3,000 votes when the race was called on Friday. Ms. Boebert, who amplified President Trump’s false claims of a stolen election in 2020, has not yet conceded. Her lawyer suggested last week that Ms. Boebert would request a recount.

Democrats flooded the airwaves in the district with more than $7 million worth of ads, outspending Republicans by more than 23 to 1, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Many of the ads fixed on Ms. Boebert’s polarizing nature and past scandals, with one calling her “uniquely unfit.” Another ad contrasted Ms. Laubacher’s profile as a Navy veteran and mother of five with headlines about Ms. Boebert.

“Lauren Boebert flips out over ‘Beetlejuice’ groping footage,” the chyron read in one clip, referring to Ms. Boebert’s ejection from a Denver theater in 2023. Another showed Ms. Boebert cursing at the person filming.

“Like so many of us, Eileen is done with the extremists in both parties,” a narrator said in the ad, which was run by Ms. Laubacher’s campaign. “Maybe the best way to break through the noise is a little less talking and more listening.”

Democrats had viewed Ms. Boebert as vulnerable in the closing stretch of this year’s race, as her once-close alliance with President Trump became a liability among voters who blamed his administration for high gas prices and other affordability concerns.

Ms. Boebert, first elected in 2020, broke with Mr. Trump at times during the past year, particularly over her calls to release files related to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. And she drew the president’s anger by campaigning for Representative Thomas Massie, the Kentucky Republican who became a nuisance for Mr. Trump.

After the election, Ms. Boebert declined to blame Mr. Trump for Republicans’ blowout losses, though she said she was “very frustrated with the war.” She told reporters this week that the Trump administration should have gone further to deport immigrants who were in the United States illegally and that Republican lawmakers “could have done a lot more.” Ms. Boebert did not respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Laubacher ran on a centrist platform but hammered Ms. Boebert for her votes against resolutions directing Mr. Trump to end the war in Iran or seek congressional approval. She also centered a promise to protect rural hospitals in the wake of Medicaid cuts.

Ms. Laubacher served in the National Security Council for two years during the Biden administration, and earlier in her career she worked as a Navy intelligence officer and served in the Navy Reserves. She was promoted to the rank of rear admiral in 2018.

“I don’t answer to a political party,” Ms. Laubacher said in a statement declaring victory on Monday. “I answer to the people of the 4th district and I’ll work with anyone and everyone, including President Trump, Republicans, and Democrats to get things done for Colorado.”

item.title: Russia Revives Demand That NATO Retrench to Secure Ukraine Deal
item.description:
Two months before Russia invaded Ukraine in early 2022, it issued a series of far-reaching demands, including that NATO pull its troops back to positions they held in 1997, before the Western alliance expanded toward Russia’s borders.

Now, in closed-door negotiations with President Trump’s envoys this week about how to end the war in Ukraine, the Russians have revived that stance — in some cases word for word — in an effort to attain a larger victory after five years and hundreds of thousands of deaths.

Moscow’s unyielding position was laid out in a paper that Russian officials circulated this week, according to a copy obtained by The New York Times from a person involved in the talks.

The paper, whose authenticity was confirmed by another person with knowledge of the negotiations, shows that President Vladimir V. Putin has scarcely budged on his core objectives after more than 20 months of diplomacy by the Trump administration to end the conflict.

Russia’s demands that NATO pull back forces from its eastern flank in Poland and the Baltics thrust the question of European security into the heart of the negotiations over Ukraine. And they detail the objective behind Mr. Putin’s public statements. The Russian leader has continually insisted that what he calls the “root causes” of the war — Russia’s wide-ranging grievances with both NATO and Ukraine — be addressed before he stops fighting.

The document also underscores how the economic inducements that Mr. Trump’s envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have offered Mr. Putin have yet to secure concessions from Moscow. To critics, the United States risks enabling Mr. Putin’s long-running attempt to reassert a Soviet-era sphere of influence as far away as Central Asia.

Russia’s decision to stake out this expansive position comes as Mr. Putin is set to sit down with Mr. Trump next week in Shenzhen, China, at an annual meeting of the Asia-Pacific regional economies. It will be the second time the two men will have met in Mr. Trump’s second term.

The Russian document, dated Nov. 10, provides new details on the hard-line stance that the Kremlin took in this week’s talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. It was the first time since February that U.S., Russian and Ukrainian officials had all met face-to-face, and the first such session since the Trump administration mounted a new push this fall to address Russia’s demands over European security in the Ukraine negotiations.

The document represents Russia’s opening position, and Russian officials in the talks signaled that Mr. Putin could still be flexible, according to the two people involved in the talks, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the sensitive discussions.

But Russian officials in Abu Dhabi made clear that they saw the Cold War, and the Soviet-led alliance at the time known as the Warsaw Pact, as a model for how Europe could look after the war in Ukraine ends. In the decades after World War II, Europe became the focal point of confrontation between nuclear superpowers, with the threat of war hanging over the continent.

But the Russians argued in Abu Dhabi that the separate U.S. and Soviet regions of influence of that era, and the communications and understandings that went along with that arrangement, actually reduced the risk of conflict, according to people present for their remarks.

It remains to be seen how far Moscow will get with that argument.

A U.S. official said that Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner had told the Russians that much had changed since December 2021, when their country demanded a new treaty that would end most NATO military activity across much of Eastern and Central Europe.

The Americans urged the Russians to look toward the future, according to the U.S. official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the negotiations. Mr. Trump’s envoys, the official said, are open to new proposals from Moscow that would include concrete steps by Russia to reduce tensions.

A spokesman for Mr. Putin did not respond to a request for comment on Friday.

Mr. Trump’s envoys are now working to allay fears that they will negotiate a sweeping deal with Mr. Putin over the heads of Europe and Ukraine.

After the Abu Dhabi meeting, Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff traveled to Moscow to meet with Mr. Putin on Thursday.

There, Mr. Kushner told Mr. Putin in the on-camera portion of the meeting that Russia, Ukraine, Europe and the United States had already made progress on “long-term security” issues. But Mr. Putin later told the Americans that Russia’s 2021 proposal for a NATO pullback still reflected “our vision of the pillars of an indivisible security architecture,” Yuri Ushakov, the Russian president’s foreign policy adviser, told reporters after the meeting.

From Moscow, the U.S. envoys went to Dublin on Thursday, where they debriefed President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine. Afterward, Mr. Kushner said that “we cannot conclude this deal without Europeans being at the table.”

But the fact that Russia’s opening position on European security this week remained virtually unchanged from five years ago illustrates the scale of the challenge of finding a compromise that will get Mr. Putin to end his war.

This week’s paper spelling out Russia’s position carries no letterhead or signature — it is a “non-paper,” in diplomatic parlance, meant to lay out one side’s views unofficially. Echoing Russia’s December 2021 demands, it says NATO countries must rule out the further expansion of their alliance and as well as “any military activity” in Ukraine and elsewhere in “Eastern Europe, in the South Caucasus and in Central Asia.”

The document shows that if anything, Mr. Putin has doubled down on some of his positions. In 2021, Russia wanted NATO to drop its “nuclear sharing” arrangements that had long allowed U.S. allies in Europe to benefit from the protection of American nuclear weapons. Now, the paper shows, Russia also wants France and Britain to rule out the possibility that they would use their nuclear weapons to protect other European countries, a concept that has been actively discussed in Europe in the past year, partly because of concerns about Mr. Trump’s willingness to come to NATO’s aid.

The paper also seeks to choke off aid to Ukraine, foreseeing an end to “the supply of any type of Western weapons and military equipment and products to Ukraine.” Russia would only approve of Ukraine’s joining the European Union, it says, if Ukraine does not participate in the bloc’s common defense policy.

And, mirroring Russia’s 2021 demands ahead of the invasion, the paper says Russia wants NATO to pull back its troops and bases to the alliance’s 1997 borders, before it began to expand into Central and Eastern Europe — a step that would weaken the ability of the alliance’s most vulnerable members, such as Poland and the ex-Soviet Baltic countries of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, to defend themselves.

In recent days, as word of Russia’s hard-line positions rippled out of Abu Dhabi, some European leaders were quick to reject them as nonstarters. Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland said on Thursday that “accepting Russia’s conditions would mean a direct threat to Poland’s security.”

“It is clear that they are unacceptable not only to Ukraine but, above all, to Europe, and certainly to countries such as Poland,” Mr. Tusk said in Dublin.

The talks in Abu Dhabi also included Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, the top American military commander in Europe. General Grynkewich, who is also the senior NATO commander, had a lively back-and-forth with Russian officials during the talks, pushing Russian officials to explain their concerns in Europe, according to two people in the room.

Capt. Arlo Abrahamson, a spokesman for General Grynkewich, said the general had attended the talks in his capacity as the head of U.S. European Command to provide military advice for U.S. leadership, but declined to comment given the sensitivity of the negotiations.

The revived Russian demands have come as Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner renewed their push in recent months to fulfill Mr. Trump’s promise to end the war in Ukraine. In doing so, the envoys have deepened talks about possible business deals with Russia and decided to engage with Mr. Putin’s longstanding efforts to negotiate a new European “security architecture.”

Previously, Ukraine’s supporters have said they were only willing to hold such negotiations with Russia after it ended its invasion.

But the circumstances have changed. Luc Frieden, the prime minister of Luxembourg, said in an interview that it was “natural” for the Americans to talk to the Russians and Ukrainians together.

“But they also talk about the future of Europe,” he went on. “We say, ‘Well, you cannot talk about the future of Europe without us being at the table.’”

Steven Erlanger contributed reporting.

item.title: Meet the Navy Veteran Who Just Beat Lauren Boebert
item.description:
Eileen Laubacher put 40,000 miles on her campaign car visiting ranching towns and rural hospitals across eastern Colorado as she tried to persuade Republican voters to dump their congresswoman, the hard-right firebrand Lauren Boebert.

Ms. Laubacher, a Navy veteran and former Republican, was a first-time Democratic candidate hoping to oust a gun-toting icon of the MAGA movement in Colorado’s reddest congressional district. Even some of her own supporters worried it was a losing fight.

But on Friday, The Associated Press declared Ms. Laubacher the winner in the unexpectedly close race.

She called her win a testament to showing up in rural towns and other places where voters felt ignored and ill-served by both major political parties. But she acknowledged she had a lot of work ahead to keep her Republican-leaning district on her side.

“We have a lot to deliver on,” Ms. Laubacher said in an interview from Washington, where she spent Monday in an orientation with other newly elected House members. “Just because we won this election doesn’t mean things have gotten better for people. Groceries haven’t gotten cheaper. The war in Iran is still happening.”

Ms. Laubacher campaigned on cutting costs, ending President Trump’s tariffs and reducing taxes on the middle class. A retired rear admiral, she pitched herself as a service-minded suburban mother of five and assailed Ms. Boebert as a walking scandal who had harmed farmers and veterans in her rural district.

For Democrats, it has long paid to square off with Ms. Boebert, a conservative lightning rod whose opponents invariably raise donations from Democratic partisans across the country. Ms. Laubacher brought in $13.7 million to defeat Ms. Boebert. The incumbent raised $1.2 million.

Ms. Laubacher is the third Democrat to flip a Republican-held congressional seat in an increasingly blue Colorado. Republicans held four of the state’s eight House seats before the midterms, but the only Republican left standing is Representative Jeff Hurd, who represents Colorado’s rural Western Slope, the district Ms. Boebert first represented but abandoned when she came within 546 votes of defeat in 2022.

Ms, Boebert’s adopted district stretches from Denver’s fast-growing exurbs to farming and ranching towns along Colorado’s eastern plains, a seemingly impenetrable conservative redoubt.

But Ms. Laubacher spent the past year and a half crisscrossing the district, which was hit by the same economic headwinds that softened Republican support in neighboring Kansas. Over the fall, Democrats and political analysts began to think that Ms. Boebert could be vulnerable because of her close ties to Mr. Trump and his unpopular policies on tariffs and the Iran war.

Ms. Boebert clashed with Mr. Trump over the release of government files on the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and Mr. Trump’s veto of a clean-water project for her parched district. Mr. Trump ultimately endorsed Ms. Boebert and held a tele-rally for her in October.

Ms. Laubacher courted suburban voters frustrated with high prices and Ms. Boebert’s personal antics. She also made inroads with rural voters angry about the high price of diesel and fertilizer.

In her campaign ads, Ms. Laubacher sat at a kitchen table discussing strained family budgets while a split-screen image showed security-camera footage of the evening in 2023 when Ms. Boebert and a companion were kicked out of a Denver theater for disrupting a performance of the musical “Beetlejuice.”

“She is not a serious person,” Ms. Laubacher said of Ms. Boebert.

At times, she sounded more like a moderate Republican than a party-line Democrat. During a debate, she said she would not vote to impeach the president. She said she supported a balanced budget, and called the $40 trillion national debt “terrible and tragic.” On Monday, she declined to say whom she might support for House speaker.

Meg Furlow, the Democratic chairwoman in Douglas County, said Ms. Laubacher showed up everywhere in the district, even when it still seemed like her campaign was a long shot.

On Monday, Ms. Furlow said Democrats in Douglas County, where Ms. Laubacher lives, were all still in shock.

“We’ve always thought it was possible, but maybe a pipe dream,” Ms. Furlow said.

Ms. Laubacher’s campaign said she had visited all 21 counties in the district, knocked on 25,000 doors and held 120 public events. She sat down with voters at green-chile harvests, veterans’ meetings and small Republican towns where Democrats rarely campaign.

Steve Nein, a farmer, retired banker and one of the few Democrats in rural Sedgwick County, near the Colorado-Nebraska state line, said he had been impressed when Ms. Laubacher showed up to speak to a room filled with Republicans and independent voters.

“At least they were listening,” Mr. Nein said. “It was an uphill battle.”

Ms. Laubacher said her campaign had framed a local newspaper article about how many people had attended that meeting. It was one moment when she began to think she might win.“

They were frustrated and felt ignored by elected officials,” Ms. Laubacher said. “They were tired of promises that never materialize. I thought to myself, this is where it’s going to matter.”

item.title: Supreme Court Set to Hear Trump’s Ban on Asylum Claims at Border
item.description:
The Supreme Court announced on Friday that it will review the legality of the Trump administration’s policy of categorically denying asylum claims from people crossing the southern border, taking up another major test of the president’s immigration agenda.

On President Trump’s first day back in office, he effectively shut down the ability of people fearing torture and persecution to apply for asylum protections at the border and then remain in the United States, declaring there was an “invasion” along the southern border. In a proclamation, he invoked what he called “the inherent right and duty of the executive branch to defend our national sovereignty.”

Immigration rights group quickly challenged the proclamation, and lower courts have found it to be illegal. But it has still largely been in force under a temporary court order. The Supreme Court case is expected to be the culmination of years of litigation over the ability of the government to prohibit migrants from claiming asylum at the border.

This Supreme Court term, which began in October and will conclude next summer, is shaping up to be dominated by Mr. Trump’s aggressive immigration policies. In December, the court will review the administration’s efforts to deport immigrants to so-called third countries where they have no ties, including nations that have faced allegations of human rights abuses. Next year, the court will consider the administration’s policy of indefinitely detaining immigrants who crossed the border illegally years ago.

In the asylum case the justices accepted on Friday, a central question is whether the president can override immigration law set by Congress. During the first Trump administration, officials struggled to come up with restrictive asylum policies at the border that would survive judicial scrutiny.

In his second term, the president adopted the prohibition on asylum claims at the border and has been fighting over the policy in court. D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, told the justices in court filings that their intervention was “urgently warranted” in part because the policy was Mr. Trump’s “main tool for stemming an unprecedented crisis of uncontrolled illegal entry.”

Mr. Trump’s initial proclamation was followed by guidance from the Department of Homeland Security that blocked people from applying for asylum who had crossed illegally.

As a result, the number of people crossing the southern border illegally has dropped to levels not seen in decades. Border Patrol agents made just over 6,000 arrests in June 2025, for instance, according to figures from the Department of Homeland Security. During the height of such crossings during the Biden administration, more than 200,000 people crossed in December 2023.

The immigrant rights groups brought the initial legal challenge on behalf of more than a dozen people who had been detained or removed from the United States without their asylum claims being addressed.

Many of those people had experienced political persecution in their home countries of Afghanistan, Cuba, Egypt, Peru and Turkey, according to court filings. Their lawyers said some were subjected to “traditional torture” at the hands of those governments.

“For nearly two years, the Trump administration’s unlawful asylum shutdown has deprived people seeking safety of their rights, placing vulnerable families, children and adults in harm’s way,” Melissa Crow, the director of litigation at the Center for Gender and Refugee Studies, said in a statement on Friday after the court had accepted the case.

She urged the justices to follow the lead of lower courts and find that the president “cannot unilaterally rewrite our immigration laws and defy the will of Congress to get its way.”

In July 2025, Judge Randolph D. Moss of Federal District Court for the District of Columbia ruled against the Trump administration’s asylum policy, finding that the Constitution and federal immigration law did not give Mr. Trump the expansive authority he claimed.

A divided appeals court panel in April largely upheld Judge Moss’s decision and rejected the administration’s view that it could “unilaterally and heedlessly return individuals even to countries where they will most certainly face persecution.”

The 2-to-1 decision from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia said Mr. Trump had to follow requirements outlined in the Immigration and Nationality Act and could not categorically deny asylum claims from people crossing from Mexico into the United States.

Zach Montague and Matt Schwartz contributed reporting.

item.title: Cargo Ship Crashes Into Docked Riverboat in New Orleans
item.description:
Search and rescue efforts were underway in New Orleans after a cargo ship struck a docked riverboat with nearly 130 people on board on Friday afternoon, the authorities said.

An asphalt tanker crashed into the riverboat, the American Heritage, around 12:30 p.m. on Friday, Kimberly Curth, a spokeswoman for the Port of New Orleans, said in a statement.

The riverboat had been docked for two hours on the Mississippi River outside of 1350 Port of New Orleans Place, Ms. Curth said, and was just beginning to unload passengers.

After the boat was struck, those on board were brought inside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building for triaging.

Local news video showed a capsized boat leaning against a dock.

A representative for the City of New Orleans said in a statement that search and rescue efforts were ongoing, and that multiple individuals had been rescued.

It was not immediately clear how many people had been rescued or their conditions.

“We are in close coordination with the U.S. Coast Guard and local authorities,” a spokeswoman for American Cruise Lines, which operates the boat, said in a statement. “Guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved. We will share more information as it becomes available.”

Gov. Jeff Landry said on social media that his office was aware of the crash and that he was headed to New Orleans.

The American Heritage can accommodate up to 150 guests, according to American Cruise Lines. It has a glass-enclosed restaurant, guest lounges and a fitness center.

“Public safety agencies are coordinating response efforts, with the immediate priority being the safety and rescue of those involved,” the New Orleans statement said. “This remains an active and developing incident.”

Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel are on scene, officials said.

This is a breaking news story. Check back for more developments.

item.title: The Numbers Behind a Stunning Upset in Mississippi
item.description:
To pull off Mississippi’s first Democratic Senate victory in more than four decades — in a state Donald J. Trump won by nearly 23 percentage points just two years ago — Scott Colom couldn’t simply ride a shifting national mood over the finish line.

A win would require high turnout among Black voters, who make up nearly 40 percent of the state’s population, and inroads with white voters. It also would not hurt if his opponent, Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, did worse than other Republicans on the ballot, as she had in the past.

In the end, he achieved all of that and more. Mr. Colom is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Mississippi since John C. Stennis, a staunch segregationist who opposed civil rights for much of his tenure. He will also be the first Black man to hold the position since the Reconstruction era. In a year of upheaval for the Senate, Mr. Colom’s win stood above the rest as Mississippi was the reddest seat flipped by a Democrat.

As in other Southern states this year, Black turnout in Mississippi was high. Voters in numerous majority-Black counties turned out at rates nearly as high as the 2024 presidential election — a remarkable achievement in a midterm. In some majority-Black neighborhoods, more voters turned out for this election than did so in 2024, even though that election featured the first Black woman presidential nominee.

Note: Data is as of noon Eastern time on Nov. 13.

Sources: The Associated Press, U.S. Census Bureau.

Christine Zhang/The New York Times

The Black share of the Mississippi electorate rose to 33 percent in 2026, compared with 30 percent two years ago, according to Times Voter Trends, which estimates how demographic groups voted using a variety of data sources. Black voters in the state are overwhelmingly Democratic, and 91 percent of them supported Mr. Colom. An increase of a few percentage points in the Black share of the electorate translates to large gains for the party.

Mr. Colom also won an estimated 25 percent of white voters in Mississippi, no small feat in one of the most racially polarized states in the country. White voters there were more Republican than white voters in any other state in 2020 and 2024, according to Times Voter Trends, with just 16 percent of them backing Joseph R. Biden Jr. or Kamala Harris.

The strongest county-level shift toward Mr. Colom occurred in DeSoto County, a suburban area near Memphis where the Black population has grown rapidly in recent years. The county backed Mr. Colom by seven percentage points, a 31-point swing from its 2024 presidential margin.

Mr. Colom also did particularly well with younger voters, winning that group by 30 percentage points, according to Times Voter Trends. In a precinct near Jackson State University, the margin was extreme: Of the 376 votes reported thus far, just one was for Ms. Hyde-Smith.

While Mr. Colom will be the third Black senator from Mississippi, he is the first to be elected by voters in the state. His predecessors, Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce, were elected by the Mississippi Legislature during Reconstruction.

Mr. Revels’s path to the Senate was not easy: It took several ballots across days of voting to decide the winner. At the time, Mississippi’s population was 54 percent Black and the Legislature was about 25 percent Black. The state’s Black legislators united behind Mr. Revels, hoping that his election would be a “weakening blow against color-line prejudice,” as he later said. When Mr. Revels arrived in Washington, Democratic senators disputed the validity of his election, but the chamber voted 48 to 8 to seat him.

Mr. Colom’s path was more straightforward, with a delay resulting from a very close election that could not be called until the state had accounted for outstanding mail-in and provisional ballots.

For as surprising as Mr. Colom’s victory has been, it is not unheard of for a modern Democrat to be competitive in a statewide contest in Mississippi. Gov. Tate Reeves, a Republican, won by five percentage points in 2019 and only three points in 2023. The state elected a Democratic attorney general as recently as 2015. But this Senate race flew under the radar. No election forecaster rated it as closer than “likely Republican” — a fact that Mr. Colom has criticized — and not a single nonpartisan poll was conducted in the state.

The ingredients for an upset, however, were there.

In addition to strong turnout among Black voters and a significant shift to the left by white and younger voters, a large factor in Mr. Colom’s victory was Ms. Hyde-Smith’s continuing her history of underperforming other Republicans. Her margin of victory in the 2018 special election for Senate was 11 percentage points less than that of Roger Wicker, the other senator from Mississippi, who won his re-election bid that year. In her successful 2020 bid to retain her seat, she ran seven percentage points behind Mr. Trump’s margin, the largest gap of any incumbent Republican senator.

This year, she lost to Mr. Colom by about half a percentage point, even as Republicans carried the statewide House vote by five points. She struggled the most, relative to other Republicans, in the whiter, eastern half of the state, including Oktibbeha County, home to Mississippi State University. Mr. Colom serves as district attorney there.

item.title: No Criminal Charges for Driver of Truck That Plowed Into Crowd in Kansas
item.description:
After a weekslong investigation into a driver whose truck plowed into a crowd on a soccer field in Kansas, killing two people and injuring 10 others, a prosecutor has announced that no criminal charges would be filed.

The events on Oct. 17 were a tragedy and a mistake, the district attorney said, but the evidence was insufficient to prove that the driver had intended to hurt anyone.

“Not everybody may be at peace with this decision,” Marc Bennett, the district attorney of Sedgwick County, said at a news conference on Thursday.

The driver of the car had found a parking spot at a sports complex in Wichita and appeared to have fallen asleep in the driver’s seat before the vehicle jumped a curb and accelerated onto a soccer field full of people, according to a report released Thursday by Mr. Bennett.

The driver, a 34-year-old woman, has not been publicly identified. The two people who died were Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both of McPherson, Kan.

The report said that there was no evidence that the driver of the car had been impaired by any substance or had experienced a medical emergency. It remains unclear whether the truck was in gear when she fell asleep.

“The notion that I could establish and prove beyond a reasonable doubt that she did this intentionally is just simply not there,” Mr. Bennett said.

Mr. Bennett described the episode as a “an act of negligence,” but he added that Kansas does not have a negligent homicide statute. “It’s not on the books,” he said.

He added that given the absence of clear intent or recklessness, the case also did not meet the legal criteria for a charge of vehicular homicide, a misdemeanor.

On the morning of Oct. 17, the driver left Garden City, Kan., at 7 a.m. with her three children in the car, the district attorney’s report said. Around 10:40, she arrived at the Stryker Sports Complex, where her two younger children, both 11, had soccer games.

After that, the family left the complex and visited two fast food restaurants and another business in the area. The report said that they returned to the complex for another game in the afternoon, and the driver told her children that she would take a nap. Her older daughter, 14, pulled a sun shade over the windshield. The younger daughter fell asleep in the back seat, officials said, and the son left to play soccer.

The vehicle, a Chevrolet Silverado Trail Boss truck, was stationary for about 46 minutes before it jolted over a seven-inch concrete curb at roughly 3:20 p.m. and onto a part of the field where spectators had gathered, the report said.

“The driver, whose chair was still fully reclined, told detectives she awoke to her daughters’ screams, the feeling of the truck moving, and the sounds of people screaming outside the truck,” the report said, adding that she had struggled to remove the sun shade from the windshield.

The report said that the truck’s brake lights had activated eight seconds after the car began to move.

Witnesses described the woman as “sleepy,” “unsure,” and “crying hysterically,” the report said. Witnesses also said that they heard her apologize multiple times, and one quoted her as saying: “I never should have come.”

According to the report, the woman had borrowed the truck, her husband’s, that morning, because the tires on her own vehicle had been losing air, and she was worried about whether she could safely make the nearly four-hour drive to Wichita.

The woman cooperated with the police, the report said, and a toxicology report found “no presence of any impairing substances in her blood.” There was also no evidence that the woman had suffered a medical emergency, Mr. Bennett said. His office declined further comment.

At the news conference, Mr. Bennett said that investigators had used a vehicle with the same make and model as the woman’s truck to recreate the scene in an effort to understand why the car had jumped the curb. He said it was possible that the driver had failed to put the truck into park before she took a nap, and then shifted in her sleep, pressing the accelerator.

Joe Sullivan, the chief of the Wichita Police Department, said at the news conference that the deaths had weighed heavily on the community, as well as on the families of the boy and the man who were killed.

“While nothing shared today can undo the loss or lessen the pain experienced by those most affected,” he said, “we hope this update provides a better understanding of what happened, and confidence that every reasonable effort has been made to uncover the truth.”

Cole’s father, Chris Adrian, has said that his family was heartbroken by the loss and described his son as “an incredible kid” who “could put a smile on anyone’s face.” On Friday, he declined to comment about the prosecutor’s decision.

Family members of Mr. Schafer and lawyers representing the people injured could not be reached for comment.

Maia Spoto contributed reporting.

item.title: Last Ground Stop, in 2023, Came After a Pilot Warning System Went Down
item.description:
Nationwide ground stops are exceptionally rare in the United States, but they are not a distant memory for many travelers.

The last nationwide ground stop came in the early morning of Jan. 11, 2023, and lasted around 90 minutes. The disruption came after a system to alert pilots of real-time dangers went down.

The NOTAM alerts, short for Notice to Air Missions, include updates on hazards like closed runways, airspace restrictions and signal disruptions. The F.A.A. said at the time there was no evidence the outage was caused by a cyberattack. The agency ordered airlines to halt departing flights just before 7:30 a.m., and the pause was lifted about 9 a.m. Flights already airborne were allowed to land at their destinations.

But the travel headaches spilled over to many passengers as airlines struggled to get their schedules back on track. By that afternoon, about 9,000 flights had been delayed and 1,300 had been canceled.

More than two decades earlier, the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks led to what was at the time an unprecedented ground stop. All airborne planes were ordered to land at the closest available airport.

item.title: Democrats Vie for Support in Race for Top Senate Job
item.description:
The Democratic battle for Senate majority leader intensified on Friday as Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland put aside his presidential ambitions to push forward in his campaign to challenge Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the current leader, and lined up supporters.

Appearing at a Democratic event in Denver on the future of the party, Mr. Van Hollen, who announced his challenge on Thursday night, said that he had ruled out a presidential run in 2028 after the sweeping Democratic wins on Nov. 3. Some Democrats had suggested that Mr. Van Hollen was jumping into the majority leader contest to raise his visibility and court progressive voters ahead of 2028, but he said that was not the case.

“I believe that the size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call of the American people,” Mr. Van Hollen said in disclosing that he was no longer pursuing a White House bid. “I think this is a really important moment for our country, and that we can’t go back to business as usual in the United States Senate.”

He also gained some public backing from senators who will decide the contest, even as he acknowledged he was the “underdog” in the race against Mr. Schumer, who was a key architect and funder of the successful Democratic effort to retake the Senate and has led Democrats there since 2016.

Senator Jeff Merkley, the Oregon Democrat in line to be chairman of the Environment and Public Works Committee, said he was supporting Mr. Van Hollen, posting on social media that he had seen him “rally support for the people against the powerful time and time again.”

Also endorsing Mr. Van Hollen on social media was Peggy Flanagan, the senator-elect from Minnesota, who wrote that Mr. Van Hollen “is the leader and fighter we need to bring about real change.” She was among the newly elected members who had campaigned on calls for a leadership change.

Still, Mr. Van Hollen, who has said he has “more than 10” backers, was believed to be significantly trailing Mr. Schumer in building support for the job. Even before he had an opponent, Mr. Schumer had collected enough commitments from his colleagues to return him for another two-year term as leader, aides said. He remains widely expected to prevail in the secret-ballot election, set for Dec. 1.

With progressive activists and some labor groups stepping up their campaigns on behalf of Mr. Van Hollen, many senators have refrained from making public declarations on what will ultimately be a private vote as a way of staying out of the line of fire.

Funding for the war in Iran is emerging as a central difference in the leadership fight, with Mr. Van Hollen demanding that Democrats withhold support for any money for the military operation even if it means shutting down the government when the current spending authority expires on Dec. 11.

Mr. Schumer has not embraced that tactic. While he has declared that he intends to force an end to the war, he and other leading Democrats have been assessing how to proceed on the funding plan. They have been weighing a temporary extension with some restrictions on the military money until early 2027, when they would hold the majority and likely be able to exert more leverage against the Trump administration.

Despite the unpopularity of the war and the role it played in the Democrats’ election sweep, many Democratic senators are leery of a widespread government shutdown heading into the holidays, fearing it would be difficult to end once it started and would upend their plans for an aggressive start to their new majority in January.

But Mr. Van Hollen said Friday that Democrats needed to be bolder on the war.

“Right now, under our current leadership, we have a situation where they’re not willing to use the most important power we have to end a war, which is to defund it,” Mr. Van Hollen said in Denver.

As they prepared for a takeover, some Democrats also privately raised the idea that the election should be held earlier than Dec. 1, to avoid having the party spend the next few weeks embroiled in a messy internal fight.

In his statement on Thursday endorsing Mr. Schumer, Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii, who is unopposed in his effort to be elected the No. 2 Democrat in the leadership, said: “We have no time to waste. We must move quickly to vote, unify, and get to work.”

Democrats could vote to move up the election now that the field appears set.

One point that many senators are embracing is a shift in communication strategy that elevates their new members, a significant change in an institution where newcomers are traditionally neither seen nor heard.

item.title: 5 Takeaways From Biden’s Memoir: The Debate, Dropping Out and Advice From Romney
item.description:
Former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., at times defiant and defensive, describes his fateful decision to run for re-election in 2024, his immediate reaction to the debate that derailed his campaign and his exasperation with Prime Minister of Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel in a new memoir, “Promise Me, America.”

Here are five takeaways from the 480-page book, scheduled to be released on Tuesday, at what would have been the rough midpoint of Mr. Biden’s second term. The 83-year-old former president, who has aggressive prostate cancer, has scaled back promotion of the memoir because of his condition.

Mr. Biden writes that he solidified his decision to run for re-election after discussing the idea with top advisers at the White House in 2023.

The reception, he recalls, was supportive and unanimous. At the time of the meeting, Mr. Biden writes, the campaign was already starting to kick into gear: He had TV ads and an announcement prepared.

“We went around the room,” writes Mr. Biden, who was just past his 80th birthday, had a drooping approval rating and had once portrayed his presidency as a bridge to the next generation of Democrats. “Everyone offered their thoughts on the race. Everyone was in. There was no demurral or dissent. I was in.”

In her own memoir published last year, “107 Days,” former Vice President Kamala Harris said Mr. Biden’s decision to run again was “recklessness” and that she should “perhaps” have advised him against it. But Ms. Harris wrote that she was in “the worst position to make the case.”

In his book, Mr. Biden writes that he was on top of the issues and that he had showed strength in the primary by gliding to the nomination over a long-shot bid from a third-term Minnesota congressman, Dean Phillips.

After his disastrous debate performance against Donald J. Trump in June 2024, Mr. Biden appeared at a watch party with the first lady, Dr. Jill Biden, who declared that he had done well.

“You answered every question,” she said as a stone-faced Mr. Biden looked on, half-smiling. “You knew all the facts.”

Privately, Mr. Biden immediately told Ms. Biden that he had bungled the debate.

“‘Well, I screwed that up,’” Mr. Biden told his wife, he writes, adding that he had used harsher language. He knew onstage that he was “having a terrible night,” he writes.

After the debate, he also promptly sought an assessment from Ron Klain, his chief of staff, he writes.

“Not good,” Mr. Klain told him.

During the debate, Mr. Biden had memorably declared that “We finally beat Medicare,” a line that prompted Mr. Trump to say, “He beat it to death.”

“What I meant to say,” Mr. Biden writes, “was, ‘We finally beat Big Pharma.’”

His performance led to a month of Democratic hand-wringing until Mr. Biden dropped out of the race.

During his abridged book tour, Mr. Biden has downplayed the history-altering debate. “It didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential,” he told People magazine.

Mr. Biden says that Mr. Trump’s “answers about his responsibility for January 6, and his refusal to say he would accept the results of the upcoming election, were disqualifying.”

And Mr. Biden notes that other presidents had bad debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate,” Mr. Biden writes. “As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me.”

Mr. Biden recalls meeting with Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader, at Mr. Biden’s beach house in Delaware about a week before dropping out of the race. In an emotional conversation, Mr. Schumer urged Mr. Biden to withdraw.

“I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race,” Mr. Biden writes. “Loyalty matters to me.”

A representative for Mr. Schumer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Biden was also pressured by Representative Nancy Pelosi of California, the former House speaker. He writes that she told him that there were “no polls” that showed he had “any chance.”

The calls for Mr. Biden to drop out continued to grow. He learned, he writes, that Senator Patty Murray of Washington planned to release a letter surfacing major Democratic defections.

“This weighed heavily on me, because even at that point, not a lot of leaders had been willing to put their names to a call for me to withdraw,” Mr. Biden writes.

Mr. Biden writes that he faced a “dilemma” — and that he had a handle on the challenges facing him.

“Was I old?” he writes. “Yes. Was I able to do the job? Yes. Were voters angry about inflation? Yes. Were they angry about immigration? Yes. All tough problems. But not insurmountable ones.”

He lists a number of leading Democrats who he says wanted him to carry on the campaign. And, he writes, “I believed the Democratic rank and file were still with me.”

But eight days after the meeting with Mr. Schumer, he withdrew from the race, pressured, he writes, by “so many major voices in our party” who were “determined to force me out.”

Ms. Harris asked him several times if he was “sure” that he wanted to drop out, he writes. When he said yes, she then asked him to endorse her immediately, rather than with a delay, he recalls. About 20 minutes later, he agreed to do so, he writes. .

Mr. Biden later moved to repair his ties with Ms. Pelosi, despite what he said were her furious efforts to push him out of the race. They reconnected for lunch at an Italian restaurant, he writes, adding that they “had been through too much together to allow a rift to go un-mended.”

Mr. Biden writes at length about Mr. Netanyahu, who prosecuted a war in Gaza with U.S. support after the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, one of the most contentious periods of Mr. Biden’s presidency.

Mr. Biden says he felt Mr. Netanyahu regularly misled him. He describes a “familiar pattern” as Mr. Biden urged the Israeli government to take pains to prevent civilian casualties.

“He would promise to do more,” Mr. Biden writes, “and then another aggressive action would follow, killing more civilians.”

Mr. Biden writes that Mr. Netanyahu’s actions, like his own re-election campaign, posed a “dilemma.”

“Bibi had no qualms about making promises he had no power — or intention — to keep,” Mr. Biden writes, using the prime minister’s nickname.

The Israeli government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Biden’s handling of the U.S.-Israeli relationship divided Democrats and angered some in his own administration.

A year into his presidency, Mr. Biden writes, he invited Senator Mitt Romney, the moderate Utah Republican and former presidential nominee, for a tour of the White House.

Mr. Romney offered some advice to the aging Mr. Biden, who had started to walk in a stiff, shuffling style.

“Pump your arms,” Mr. Romney, who is four years younger than Mr. Biden, said, according to the book. The senator told the president: “You’re holding your hands stiffly by your side when you walk. Pump your arms and you’ll look more energetic and confident.”

Mr. Biden writes that he tried to follow the senator’s “good advice.”
