item.title: Trump Administration Delays Enforcement of Medicaid Work Requirement
item.description:
The Trump administration will allow states to delay enforcement of new rules requiring low-income adults to work in order to receive Medicaid coverage, according to a letter it sent on Friday to state Medicaid directors.

The announcement, which followed a recent loss in court over a key element of the work requirement, represents a major setback for a long-sought Republican reform. It comes less than two months before the work requirements were set to begin, on Jan. 1. States can now wait until July before ending coverage for people who do not meet the work requirement, the letter said.

In the letter, Dan Brillman, who oversees Medicaid at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, acknowledged the significant burden states faced in building out new, expensive software systems to track the employment of enrollees. Hospitals have prepared massive education campaigns to help patients navigate the additional paperwork.

“We have heard directly from states about their implementation timelines, impediments to successful launches at scale,” Mr. Brillman wrote in the letter.

He added that the federal government still expected states in January to begin checking whether Medicaid enrollees are working. But for six months, they will not be required to cancel coverage for people who fail to comply, Mr. Brillman said.

The work requirement was enacted in the summer of 2025 as part of Republicans’ major tax and domestic policy legislation. It requires Medicaid enrollees without disabilities or young children to prove they worked, volunteered or attended school at least 80 hours a month in order to qualify for the program or continue enrollment in it.

The new requirement was expected to lead to substantial reductions in Medicaid coverage, disqualifying not only beneficiaries without jobs but also many who worked but were tripped up by documentation challenges. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the policy would result in five million more Americans becoming uninsured over the next few years.

Democratic lawmakers fought the policy last year. Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become speaker when Democrats take over control of the House in January, has announced plans to vote on reversing the work requirement and other Medicaid cuts within the first 100 hours of the next Congress.

In court, 25 states and the District of Columbia had already won a six-month reprieve from some aspects of enforcing the work requirement. A federal judge in Massachusetts found that the Trump administration’s rules for defining who is too “medically frail” to comply with work requirements were stricter than the law allowed.

The January start date is specified in the text of the 2025 tax law. At a conference with state Medicaid officials last summer, where many expressed concerns about the timetable, Trump administration officials warned that no extensions would be coming.

“We know it’s going to be really hard for you to meet the deadline,” said Sara Vitolo, the deputy director for Medicaid. “It’s going to be hard for us. The expectation is going to be that we hit it. And that’s coming from the White House.”

The law also allows states to begin enforcing a work requirement early, and Nebraska and Montana have already begun their programs. In Nebraska, state officials estimate that more than 1,700 people have already been denied or lost Medicaid coverage due to the policy.

Christopher Rowland contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Officials Press Congress to Renew Spying Law in Lame-Duck Session
item.description:
The Trump administration pressed top lawmakers on Friday to extend a high-profile warrantless surveillance law within the next month, moving to resolve a thorny policy dispute in the last weeks of a Republican-controlled Congress.

In a letter to congressional leaders, three top national security officials in the administration — Todd Blanche, the attorney general, Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, and John Ratcliffe, the C.I.A. director — said President Trump had urged them to extend the law known as Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act now.

“As you know, Section 702 is the single most indispensable tool we have to keep our homeland and the American people safe,” they wrote. “It enables our intelligence community to detect and disrupt terrorist plots, cyber intrusions, and weapons proliferation. No other authority can replace it.”

But any push to bring a Section 702 bill to the floor — either by itself, or bundled with some larger package like the annual National Defense Authorization Act — appeared likely to set off a new round of heated contention. Privacy and civil liberties advocates in both parties have been pushing to add new limits, like requiring the government to obtain permission from a judge before deliberately gaining access to the messages of Americans swept up under the program.

In a statement, Senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat and proponent of adding more limits to the program, said the issue should wait for the next Congress, when Democrats will have control.

“It would be unconscionable for any Democrat to hand Trump powerful spying powers, right after millions of Americans told Congress to stand up to Trump’s abuses,” he said. “There is time for Congress to pass real reforms to protect Americans’ rights and ensure warrantless surveillance cannot be weaponized against law-abiding Americans.”

Because of the Senate filibuster rule, the votes of 60 senators would most likely be required to bring a Section 702 bill to the floor for an up-or-down vote in that chamber. An extensive debate over the matter could interfere with efforts by Republicans to use their remaining time in power for other purposes, like confirming judges.

A group of privacy-minded activist groups also released a joint letter on Friday urging Congress not to fold a Section 702 extension into the National Defense Authorization Act at the last minute, arguing that would be “a betrayal of the democratic process.”

Congress enacted Section 702 in 2008 to legalize a form of the Stellarwind warrantless wiretapping program, which the Bush administration secretly created after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001. It allows the government to obtain, without a warrant and from American providers like AT&T and Google, the messages of foreigners abroad — even when they are communicating with Americans.

The statute already expired in June amid a congressional impasse. Lawmakers were deadlocked over proposed new limits, Democratic pushback to Mr. Trump’s temporary appointment of an inexperienced loyalist, Bill Pulte, as acting spy chief, and Mr. Trump’s own vow to veto any FISA legislation unless lawmakers first passed an unrelated measure that would have tightened restrictions on voting.

But because of the way Congress wrote the law, the National Security Agency can legally operate the program until March 2027, when annual certification orders issued by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court are set to lapse.

The debate over Section 702 scrambles the usual partisan lines, with national-security hawks and centrists in both parties aligning against an alliance of civil liberties-minded lawmakers of both parties. That makes the politics unpredictable.

In an interview, Representative Jim Himes, a Connecticut Democrat who is expected to become the chairman of the House Intelligence Committee in January, said that he warned Mr. Ratcliffe and Mr. Clayton during a classified briefing this week that the Trump administration needed to work with lawmakers to renew Section 702 in the lame-duck session or risk contending with a new Congress that is far more skeptical of the surveillance law.

A renewal next year would look “radically different” than what might pass otherwise, Mr. Himes said he told them. He added that the new Congress was likely to impose a stronger warrant requirement on searching for information about Americans in the repository of intercepted communications, as civil libertarians want. Security agencies oppose that proposal, arguing it would hamstring the program’s effectiveness.

Trump administration officials addressed their letter to top lawmakers, including Senator John Thune, the majority leader, and Speaker Mike Johnson, along with their Democratic counterparts, Senator Chuck Schumer and Representative Hakeem Jeffries. The letter argued that obtaining a new set of annual certification orders and translating them into operating instructions takes months to complete, meaning the lawmakers should act by Dec. 9.

“To prevent a gap in critical intelligence and avoid putting our nation at risk, the government must start the 2027 renewal process by then,” they wrote.

But Don Bell, senior policy counsel at the Project on Government Oversight, called that deadline “completely arbitrary.”

“After months of refusing to engage on reforms that would protect both national security and civil liberties, the White House and surveillance hawks are terrified the next Congress will end the administration’s blank check for warrantless surveillance,” he said.

Julian E. Barnes contributed reporting.

item.title: Airports Fill Up With Stuck Families and Stranded Travelers
item.description:
Skies above America’s busiest airports were eerily empty on Friday, while terminals and baggage claim areas overflowed with confused passengers as flights were grounded across the country.

Chicago’s O’Hare, one of the nation’s busiest hubs, was a morass of confusion and frustration. Swarms of passengers attempted to rebook flights on their phones, and airline gate agents pleaded for patience as they repeated that they had no information to share.

Travelers sprawled out on the floor, settling in for what could become a long, uncomfortable night. Some headed to the city for the night, or home, abandoning their travel plans altogether.

More than 1.5 million people were scheduled to board flights departing after the Federal Aviation Administration announced a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm.

Frank Foto, 34, worried that his family would not be able to leave Chicago in time to board a cruise ship on Saturday in Miami. The trip had been planned months ago to celebrate his mother-in-law’s 60th birthday, he said.

“On the bright side, I suppose it’s better than being stuck at sea — especially with him,” Mr. Foto said, gesturing toward his infant son.

In northern Mexico, Luisa Jiménez quickly realized that the $200 tickets she had bought for a trip to see the Golden State Warriors, her favorite basketball team, play in San Antonio would go to waste. An airline agent confirmed that her flight out of Monterrey International Airport had been canceled.

“People are really upset because there’s no information,” said Ms. Jiménez, 30, as she weighed whether to fly home to southern Mexico, where she lives.

In Orlando, Fla., a family of nine heading back to Cincinnati after a trip to Disney World returned their rental car and checked out of their Airbnb, only to have to get off their flight after boarding.

“He’ll be 8 tomorrow,” Mary Hughes, 44, said of her son, Josiah. “So we need to be home, so he can have his birthday cake — not stuck in Florida.”

She didn’t know how the family could afford to extend its trip. “We don’t have any more money,” she said.

At LaGuardia Airport, passengers aboard a flight to Portland, Maine, were stuck on the ground for about four hours on Friday evening before they were assigned a gate, Becca Freeman, 40, said in a call from the plane.

This was Ms. Freeman’s second attempt to fly to Maine this week. Her first flight on Thursday was canceled because of bad weather.

The outage comes about two weeks before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest times of the year for air travel. On average, U.S. airlines are expected to fly about 2.7 million passengers each day over the holiday period, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

In Atlanta on Friday, a line of travelers waiting to retrieve their checked bags extended past three airport entrances at Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport. Many in the line had checked bags before their flights were delayed or canceled. Some had been waiting for over an hour to get them back.

Ashley Van Mills, 45, had arrived at the airport hoping to catch an evening flight to Chicago.

“We’ve been flying for I don’t know how many years, and this doesn’t happen,” she said. “It’s just the unknown that gives you an uneasy feeling.”

Reporting was contributed by Eric Adelson, Robert Chiarito, Jack Healy, Vik Jolly, Sean Keenan, Madison Malone Kircher, Niraj Chokshi, Ryley Ober and Emiliano Rodríguez Mega.

item.title: Here’s What Happens if Your Flight Is Canceled
item.description:
In the United States, if your flight is canceled, significantly delayed or changed, airlines will rebook you on another flight, or at the very least try to rebook you.

Airlines will do more for passengers when the cause of a delay or a cancellation is their fault. An air traffic control outage isn’t, which means that what passengers can expect right now is limited.

You’re also entitled to a refund if your flight is canceled, regardless of the reason, or if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and you decide not to take it.

But airlines won’t guarantee other amenities, such as a hotel room in the case of overnight cancellation, ground transportation, or meal vouchers.

In the case of a tarmac delay, airlines are required to provide passengers some assistance: water and a snack within two hours of the start of a tarmac delay, unless there are safety or security reasons preventing this, according to the Transportation Department. Airlines don’t have to serve a full meal.

In the United States, airlines have three hours, for domestic flights, to move the plane to a place where passengers can safely disembark. This is four hours for international flights. However, travelers who get off the plane run the risk of not being allowed back on it.

Waiting it out at the airport in an endless line during the current ground stop may not be the best strategy for Friday, said Jamie Larounis, a travel industry analyst.

“This won’t be a quick fix,” he said, adding that flight disruptions would likely ripple into the weekend.

Mr. Larounis said the priority for affected travelers was to get on another flight that departs in several days, booking a hotel as soon as possible if stranded outside your home city, and to consider train travel, if possible.

item.title: Mullin Says Nationwide Ground Stop Is a Telecommunication Outage
item.description:
With flights grounded across the United States, Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of Homeland Security, sought to assure the public they were not in danger even as he acknowledged the Trump administration did not know the cause of what he said was a telecommunications outage that snarled air travel.

“Do we know what has caused it yet?” said Mr. Mullin, who took the lead of the Homeland Security Department in March. “No, we’re going to go through it. But I’m not going to make assumptions.”

Standing outside the White House, Mr. Mullin said he had been inundated with questions about whether Americans were in danger. He said they were not.

“This isn’t another 9/11,” he said. “I just can’t repeat that enough. People are making that assumption.” He added: “This is a telecommunication outage.”

The Federal Aviation Administration announced the rare nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, due to what officials said was a major outage affecting its air traffic control system.

“There is no indication, and we had no reason to believe as of right now that this was a threat to the United States,” Mr. Mullin told reporters. “This was a telecommunication outage throughout F.A.A. Out of abundant caution, we have grounded all the flights, and all the flights are accounted for.”

For flights in the air, Mr. Mullin said, they would be dealt with “case by case” and there would be a “priority list” for when those flights would land at their destinations.

“There was no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us,” he said. “It’s just a telecommunication outage as of right now.”

The nationwide grounding of flights is the latest crisis that Mr. Mullin, a former senator from Oklahoma, has encountered since becoming homeland security secretary. When he took over the agency, Mr. Mullin inherited an aggressive and widely unpopular immigration crackdown that resulted in the killings of U.S. citizens.

In his remarks Friday, Mr. Mullin praised President Trump, whom he said “took a lead in this immediately, and he gave us he assets and the communication to move forward in a fast way.”

As of Friday evening, Mr. Trump had yet to comment publicly about the aviation crisis. Instead he posted on his social media site his desire to pass tax incentives to lure more motion pictures to be made in the United States.

item.title: Nvidia Scandal Prompts Questions of What It Means to Be a Spy
item.description:
Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the center of the Nvidia spying scandal, was believed to be using her affair with Nvidia’s founder to help China get around U.S. efforts to restrict access to advanced A.I. chips, people who have read U.S. intelligence reporting said.

But there remains much that intelligence agencies are still assessing about Ms. Huang including when she began working with China’s top spy agency, whether her cooperation was willing or coerced, how much direction Beijing gave her, and how much she relayed to officials there, the people said.

Her relationship with Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday, gave her potential access to crucial information about the company’s technology, Mr. Huang’s strategic thinking and his knowledge of Washington’s debates about A.I. policy.

She also had a business interest in ensuring a flow of chips to her own company, one of a number in Southeast Asia that provided Chinese tech firms with the computing power needed to train advanced artificial intelligence models.

The aftershocks of the scandal continue to play out as President Trump prepares for a trip next week to Asia, where he is scheduled to meet with President Xi Jinping of China, who has made a top priority of catching the United States in the race for A.I. dominance.

The unknowns surrounding Ms. Huang have generated intense scrutiny of how Chinese intelligence operates, prompted questions of what it means to be a spy and given backers of Mr. Huang an opening to raise questions about the extent and nature of her role.

Mr. Trump, who has viewed Mr. Huang as an important ally in his push to maintain American superiority in A.I. as well as a key driver of the U.S. economy, has defended the former Nvidia leader. On Thursday he seemed to suggest that he was less sure than are U.S. intelligence agencies that Mr. Huang had been the target of a Chinese intelligence operation.

“The big thing is, was the woman a spy, and I don’t know if that’s been determined yet,” Mr. Trump said in an interview with Stephen A. Smith, the podcaster and sports commentator, when asked if Mr. Huang should have resigned. “But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy perhaps it would be different.”

Still, the concerns in the U.S. intelligence community that Ms. Huang was spying on behalf of Beijing were taken so seriously that Mr. Trump was twice briefed on it, late last year and again this spring.

One of those briefings was by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security adviser. Mr. Rubio had overseen the drafting of a memo, dated March 30, sent to a handful of Cabinet secretaries, that detailed Ms. Huang’s close relationship with the Nvidia founder and her contacts with China’s main civilian intelligence service, the Ministry of State Security.

Mr. Trump said this week that Mr. Huang had told him he did not know Ms. Huang was tied to Chinese intelligence. Ms. Huang has not responded to outreach from The New York Times.

Ms. Huang was a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that purchased Nvidia chips and built data centers in Southeast Asia whose customers included Alibaba, the Chinese commerce giant.

The Commerce Department launched an investigation into whether Megaspeed was helping illegally divert Nvidia chips to China, an inquiry launched well before the current scandal emerged and subsequently taken over last year by the Justice Department. Authorities in Singapore also questioned Ms. Huang last year. Her current whereabouts is unknown.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a news conference on Thursday that the Justice Department has a role in investigating whether advanced chips had been sold to China in violation of U.S. export controls.

“If there are chips that shouldn’t be sold it could potentially be a violation of our export laws,” Mr. Blanche said. “That could be civil, regulatory, it could also be criminal, depending on the case. And that investigation is ongoing.”

Mr. Blanche sidestepped a question about whether the Justice Department has made an assessment about the nature of Ms. Huang’s role.

Multiple people who have reviewed the underlying U.S. intelligence said that it showed that Ms. Huang was working with the Chinese intelligence agency.

People briefed on the intelligence say it appears that she was not a trained intelligence officer but rather an “asset,” someone providing information secretly to the Ministry of State Security.

Chinese espionage is complicated. There are a range of ways that Chinese business executives can conduct espionage for the Beijing government, from simply reporting what they know to taking active direction.

U.S. intelligence agencies have confidence in their information about her interactions with Chinese intelligence services, despite all that they do not know about Ms. Huang.

Current and former officials said that Chinese business executives often believe that they cannot advance their careers without being aligned with the state. Approached by the Chinese government to collect information or prod an American company for access to high-end chips, many Chinese executives might feel they have no choice but to comply.

The U.S. intelligence community has been gathering surveillance on Ms. Huang for well over a year. She was already in a close relationship with Mr. Huang when the surveillance began, people familiar with the situation said.

Determining when Ms. Huang started providing information to the Ministry of State Security is important as American intelligence tries to better understand what details she might have gathered during her affair with Mr. Huang.

Mr. Huang stepped down from Nvidia after admitting to an affair and after the company’s board began investigating his relationship with Ms. Huang. The board pushed for Mr. Huang’s resignation not just because of the spying allegations. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported Mr. Huang had conducted another affair with an executive who reported directly to him.

item.title: Trump to Meet With Putin and Xi in China, With Nuclear Proliferation on the Agenda
item.description:
President Trump will have a joint meeting with Xi Jinping, China’s leader, and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia during a summit in China next week, a White House spokeswoman said on Friday.

It will be the first trilateral meeting the three leaders have held together, and the third meeting Mr. Trump has had with Mr. Xi in person this year. At the meeting with Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump plans to discuss the war against Iran, but is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.

Olivia Wales, the White House spokeswoman, said that Mr. Trump would also address the threat of nuclear proliferation. U.S. officials have expressed concerns about a steady buildup of China’s arsenal in recent years, and a U.S. nuclear arms control treaty with Russia expired in February.

“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Ms. Wales said in a telephone briefing with reporters.

Two senior administration officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the president’s travel plans, said that Mr. Trump would travel to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila early next week. The officials said he would then travel to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, where he will meet with Mr. Xi and then both Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin.

The officials said that Mr. Trump would be joined by the billionaire Elon Musk in Shenzhen, but added that Mr. Musk would not be part of the trilateral meeting.

Mr. Trump is prepared to discuss the “difficult” topic of Beijing’s nuclear arsenal with Mr. Xi, one of the officials said.

China maintains secretive nuclear facilities and is on track to have 1,000 nuclear warheads by 2030, producing the weapons at a pace that has worried U.S. officials and analysts. On the call, the administration officials said that they did not expect any agreements on nuclear proliferation, and characterized the talks as a starting point.

Mr. Trump said this week that he had no plans to discuss with Mr. Xi the scandal that had engulfed Jensen Huang, who until this week was the chief executive of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world. Mr. Huang stepped down from his role in the wake of revelations that he had engaged in extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe is an asset of Beijing.

The officials said that the matter involving Ms. Huang was a national security issue, and did not expect Mr. Trump to discuss it with Mr. Xi during a diplomatic meeting.

item.title: The Science One University Sacrificed to Avoid Trump’s Wrath
item.description:
Professors at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill worried how the Trump administration’s ire toward universities would affect them. But the school’s leaders thought they had a plan.

Supported by

The University of North Carolina’s chancellor tried to protect the school from the Trump administration. Work on cancer, suicide, AIDS and coronaviruses was hit anyway.

By Alan BlinderStephanie SaulIrena Hwang and Benjamin Mueller

Visuals by Mike Belleme

The reporters reviewed internal documents and recordings and interviewed dozens of people connected to U.N.C., some of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared retaliation from the Trump administration.

The professor was crying.

She had joined the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill to research race and environmental disasters. Now the Trump administration had cut off money that made much of her work possible, and university leaders had few ideas to keep it going.

Directly fighting back in the courts was not an option, administrators told a handful of professors during a video meeting in May 2025. Maybe, the officials suggested, researchers could rewrite their proposals to avoid mentioning topics that the Trump administration might find objectionable, like race.

That seemed like “whitewashing,” the anguished professor said in a recording of the meeting obtained by The New York Times.

A series examining disruption to research and discovery under Trump.

One of the university’s top research officials, Andy Johns, fought tears himself.

“There’s no part of this that feels right,” he told the group. “But right now, we have to navigate it as best we can.”

As the Trump administration pursued the most consequential reshaping of American scientific research in generations, it sought to slash funding at private universities it depicted as hotbeds of intolerance and left-leaning ideology. But the campaign was so indiscriminate that it reached far beyond the Ivy League to include many of the nation’s large public research universities.

Leaders at most of those institutions, particularly the ones accustomed to navigating complicated politics in red and purple states, concluded that suing the federal government, like Harvard had done, was not realistic. Some hunkered down, minimizing the losses where they could while remaining largely out of the fray.

U.N.C. charted a different path — one of careful conciliation.

Quiet and often noncommittal in public, the university’s chancellor, Lee Roberts, maneuvered behind the scenes on two delicate fronts. On campus, he and his fellow administrators worked to calm an increasingly enraged faculty. With an eye on Washington, they also tried nudging Trump officials away from their most destructive impulses.

Major research projects — including on cancer, infectious diseases and heart failure — were canceled or disrupted. But the university also managed to keep the vast majority of its research funding intact.

Grant money from the National Institutes of Health, the university’s largest single source of research funding, dipped early in the administration. This year, it ticked back up, even rising slightly above its Biden-era levels. The university also found new sources of federal research dollars for Trump administration interests like artificial intelligence and quantum technology.

But there was another cost. While many professors sympathized with U.N.C.’s administration, mistrust deepened on campus as professors wondered whose side their leaders were on.

In an interview this summer, Mr. Roberts acknowledged the consequences of the cuts while avoiding direct criticism of the government that was causing them.

“It’s not an exaggeration to say that we have people here who have lost their life’s work,” he said. “It’s hard to overstate how devastating that is.”

Seventeen days after Donald J. Trump’s election, Mr. Roberts trooped to a meeting of U.N.C.’s faculty council.

The group’s leader, Beth Moracco, paced before professors in a video recording posted by the university. She quoted JD Vance, who had just been elected vice president, calling universities the enemy and said she had sometimes plunged into the “rabbit hole of speculation and catastrophizing.” But she pleaded with people not to engage in “anticipatory compliance.”

Then it was Mr. Roberts’s turn.

Urbane and taciturn, he was more seasoned in Washington’s ways — and less in higher education’s — than a typical university leader. His parents, Cokie and Steven Roberts, had been among the capital’s best-known journalists. Two grandparents had served in Congress. An uncle, a lobbyist, had been so powerful in Washington that Vanity Fair christened him “King of the Hill.”

In 1990, a newspaper profile noted that Lee Roberts, at the time a Duke University student, planned to become a lobbyist himself. He wound up as a finance executive, a budget director to a Republican governor and, beginning in 2024, U.N.C.’s chancellor.

When Mr. Trump was elected again, some looked at Mr. Roberts’s résumé and saw someone who could be effective in dealing with the new administration. Others worried that he might align himself with higher education’s Republican antagonists, who had already pushed the university system to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion programs.

As Mr. Roberts faced his faculty, he agreed the university should not jump to please the incoming Trump administration. But he also counseled patience.

“There is very little that is knowable,” he said, leaning against a lectern.

U.N.C. was positioned unusually well compared with its peer universities. Mr. Trump carried North Carolina three times, and the university already had Republican-aligned board members, lobbyists and administrators. As Mr. Trump prepared to return to Washington, he picked allies of the university for influential posts; an alumnus, for example, was named deputy director of the budget office.

In Chapel Hill, a liberal oasis in a perennially contested state, many academics viewed Mr. Trump as an aspiring autocrat. But U.N.C.’s leaders thought trying to guide Trump officials, rather than fighting with them, would better protect the university.

“We’d rather be in the room before policy is developed,” said former Senator Richard Burr, a North Carolina Republican and one of the university’s Washington lobbyists.

“We’re not paid to just sit and raise hell. We’re paid to have the conversations,” said Chris McClure, the university’s chief strategic officer. Talking to Trump officials, he added, “doesn’t mean you’re accommodating.”

U.N.C. slowly made inroads. The university forged “a direct relationship” with the all-important White House budget office, talking Trump aides through the arcane process of federal grant making, Penny Gordon-Larsen, U.N.C.’s top research official, said in an interview.

Still, the stop-work orders for projects had started soon after Mr. Trump’s inauguration on Jan. 20. By the end of February, according to an internal document, there were more than two dozen, unleashing havoc and anxiety across the campus.

Even when the government wasn’t sending explicit word of cuts, money was not flowing as anticipated.

In late February, Paul Maddox, a biologist who studies cancer, was still waiting for a routine extension of a grant to improve his invention, called the Mizar TILT — a light system that enhances cell images under a microscope.

“We thought, ‘They’re not going to attack our grants. Why would they attack our grants?’” he recalled. “We just kept working as normal.”

That was in line with the advice of U.N.C. leaders, who were telling professors that funding hiccups often happened during presidential transitions.

But as the government began targeting individual universities with hundreds of millions of dollars in cuts each, U.N.C. sought reinforcements. It hired a lobbying firm whose leader, Ches McDowell, was a brother of a Republican congressman and a hunting buddy of Donald Trump Jr. (Mr. McDowell, whose brother lost his re-election bid this month, did not respond to interview requests.)

It is not clear how much it helped. U.N.C., whose leaders were spending hours each day talking with one another and trying to talk to government officials, told faculty members in April that the disruptions were “fluid and change by the day, sometimes within a day,” according to an internal summary of an event for researchers.

By then, the document said, the university had counted 75 terminations or stop-work orders.

Universities around the country were experiencing similar cuts and confusion. The Trump administration had advertised its plans to target places like Harvard and Columbia, but they were also re-examining the entire federal research apparatus. U.N.C. leaders were not certain that the school could avoid the types of blanket cuts that the administration was pursuing against other top schools.

That month, Dr. Maddox learned formally that his funding program had been shut down.

“I’d never had to fire anyone,” he said. “I had to fire all these people.”

As federal funding disappeared, researchers looked elsewhere, even soliciting donations on social media.

“We invite you to give what you can to help keep this research alive,” Jaime Slaughter-Acey, an epidemiologist, posted on LinkedIn. “Every contribution — large or small — helps us continue gathering data, mentoring students, and producing science that matters.”

In May 2025, Dr. Gordon-Larsen and her deputy, Mr. Johns, held the video call with the researchers, who were considering tapping an outside funder to help cover grants the government had cut. Dr. Gordon-Larsen and Mr. Johns were not optimistic.

Instead, they warned that the university could face dire consequences if the government decided that projects defied Mr. Trump’s orders — even if the money for them didn’t come from the government.

During the private call, though, Dr. Gordon-Larsen told professors that she had a “burning anger in my heart.”

As Abbey Hatcher, a public health researcher, listened, the we’re-in-this-together messaging frustrated her. She knew other universities were more willing to test the administration.

“I liken it to the federal government pushing us off of a plank,” she said later, “and U.N.C. tying our hands behind our backs before we go in.”

In a statement, U.N.C. denied it had limited applications for outside funding. The government eventually rescinded the language that had unnerved university officials, and several of the researchers in the video call received grants from the private funder.

But around the same time, U.N.C. was grappling for other ways to stem the federal losses. A list that circulated inside the university in May 2025 advised people to “try to avoid” more than 50 words and terms, including “climate crisis,” “disability,” “diversity,” “sexuality” and “socioeconomic.”

Ganga S. Bey, an epidemiologist, expected about $250,000 to finish a project she had worked on for years. The study focused on a group of Black residents of Jackson, Miss., to understand factors that affect heart failure.

The work was just the sort of thing the Trump administration argued was exclusionary, because of its focus on one racial group. And its funding source, a pot of money meant to promote diversity, made it even more vulnerable.

The government cut the grant, forcing Dr. Bey to lay off assistants and eliminate the final leg of the project — personal interviews with the study participants.

“You have whole research portfolios that are obliterated,” she said.

The 16-campus university system capped new hiring on June 12. By late September, nearly 150 U.N.C. grants had been terminated or targeted with stop-work orders.

Like other universities, U.N.C. had been bracing for the end of N.I.H. grant money that surged during the coronavirus pandemic. But it was still a jarring shift for a university whose research projects were worth more than $1 billion. In recent years, U.N.C. has received more than $500 million each year in N.I.H. grants, its largest source of federal funding.

In the first fiscal year under Mr. Trump, that funding declined by about $27 million, compared with the average under the Biden administration.

U.N.C.’s renowned public health school, where much of the N.I.H. money has gone, was among the hardest hit.

Still, some observers thought Mr. Roberts’s Republican-friendly strategy was having some success.

Representative Valerie Foushee, a Democrat who represents Chapel Hill in Congress, said it had seemed that the administration was perhaps giving U.N.C. “a better shake” than other schools in her district, including Duke, as Mr. Roberts and his team pursued what she called “a calculated plan.”

In September, U.N.C.’s leadership faced the faculty again, and again promised it was lobbying on their behalf.

It did not feel that way to some professors.

Andrea Azcarate-Peril, a microbiologist, said in an interview that it had often seemed like faculty members, not administrators, were the ones screaming, “this is not right.”

The university sharply limited appeals to the federal agencies imposing cuts. Even a department leader’s support for an appeal could be overruled. U.N.C. said it backed appeals most likely to succeed.

It also pointed to litigation against the Trump administration led by outside groups that could benefit researchers. And behind the scenes, though the university did not publicize it, Mr. Roberts was helping indirectly.

According to two people in the higher education industry, Mr. Roberts consulted with the Association of American Universities, a group of the nation’s top research schools, as it considered whether to fight the government in court.

Some faculty members were sympathetic to the U.N.C. administration’s plight.

Abigail Knight, an associate professor of chemistry, said the university’s leaders were doing “the best they can.” But changes have been coming so quickly, she added, “I think a lot of times they don’t know what to do.”

In its statement, U.N.C. said its highest priority had always been “championing the importance of federal research funding to the university and to the state of North Carolina.”

It added, “Carolina’s results speak for themselves and have been achieved, to date, with minimal disruption compared to peer institutions.”

In the fall, Mr. Roberts found a line he would not cross. The Trump administration had floated a “compact” for universities to sign, dangling preferential treatment for research funding in exchange for ideological loyalty.

“There is really no way that we can sign the compact as written,” he told faculty members in November, “and we don’t plan to.”

No other major university in the country signed it either.

The public stance, arguably the university’s strongest pushback to the Trump agenda to that point, gave some professors hope that U.N.C. might be getting braver about standing up to the federal government. The hope did not last.

In July 2026, one of U.N.C.’s most prominent researchers made Fox News — the sort of publicity that many university leaders desperately wanted to avoid — when Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave an interview. Peering into the camera, he cast a new spotlight on a topic that had already unleashed turmoil in Chapel Hill.

Mr. Kennedy declared to Fox that Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, when he was director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, paid Ralph Baric, one of U.N.C.’s star researchers, to develop “techniques for weaponizing Covid-19,” which he then “taught” to a collaborator in Wuhan, China, where the pandemic began. No clear evidence has ever been offered that Dr. Baric’s work helped start the pandemic, and he has denied training Wuhan scientists on such techniques.

He had spent decades in Chapel Hill, sounding the alarm about coronaviruses in China and eventually helping to find treatments and test a vaccine for Covid.

But after Mr. Trump’s second term began, Mr. Kennedy’s health department clamped down on Dr. Baric, removing him from his federal grants. U.N.C. responded by placing Dr. Baric on administrative leave, barring him from his lab and opening its own review.

This January, U.N.C. reinstated him and sent the N.I.H. a four-page defense. Dr. Gordon-Larsen told the government that she hoped it would “conclude its inquiry,” adding: “U.N.C. deeply appreciates its partnership with N.I.H. and the federal government.”

Instead, the agency intensified its scrutiny.

In May, the health department suspended Dr. Baric from federal contracts and proposed that he be barred from receiving future grants. The university again placed him on administrative leave, though it has also provided him with significant financial support for his legal defense. Days later, it announced his retirement.

The case against Dr. Baric, who declined to comment, exacerbated fears on campus. If the university had seemingly abandoned someone so important, some professors worried, who would it protect?

“You go from a hero to an antihero for no obvious reason,” said Dr. Myron S. Cohen, an H.I.V. researcher at U.N.C.

In an interview in September, Mr. Roberts paused for 11 seconds when asked whether Dr. Baric had done anything wrong. “I don’t really know if I’m the best person to answer that,” he replied.

U.N.C. later said in a statement that Dr. Baric had “left behind a legacy of consequential research that reflected both his integrity and his extraordinary intellect.” The statement added that U.N.C. “supported him since allegations first surfaced in 2020, and that support continues today.”

During the university’s first faculty council meeting this semester, U.N.C. leaders acknowledged how stressful the year had been. But, Dr. Gordon-Larsen told professors, “the positives are plenty despite the overall challenges that we’re facing.”

“Research is thriving at Carolina,” she told the professors.

The Trump administration wanted American research to shift toward more artificial intelligence, robotics and nuclear energy, and U.N.C. had just won up to $35 million to harness A.I. to better understand rare diseases.

The funding came from a federal agency focused on high-risk and high-impact breakthroughs, rather than incremental research, and it has awarded U.N.C. tens of millions more for research on neurodegenerative diseases, drug development and cancer.

By the end of the fiscal year in September, U.N.C. had received about 900 N.I.H. grant awards, around 130 fewer than the average under the Biden administration.

But even as some individual researchers and departments saw their money shrivel, the university’s overall funding from the N.I.H. was even higher than before.

The university also built, or cemented, relationships with other parts of the federal government. In July, the Pentagon picked the university as a host for a program that the government had earlier yanked from schools that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called “woke breeding grounds of toxic indoctrination.”

And in October, U.N.C. and the Justice Department signed an agreement to close 19 federal inquiries and preserve the university’s access to research money.

Other universities had reached settlements more than a year earlier. The university did not pay any fines, but it pledged to comply with the Trump administration’s views on matters like D.E.I., admissions and the punishment of student groups for actions perceived as antisemitic.

Holden Thorp, a former U.N.C. chancellor who is now editor in chief of Science, said he thought some at the university had “lulled themselves into thinking that the university was somehow immune from political power.”

Now, he said, “I think Carolina is just trying to be the best U.N.C. it can in this environment.”

The midterm election results could scramble the plan after Democrats romped to big victories in North Carolina, diminishing Republican power in Washington and Raleigh. But whether Democrats will be able to reverse the president’s policies is unclear. The White House still controls the agencies overseeing federal research funding.

The toll so far has been steep. Paul Maddox, the biologist, took a leave of absence, temporarily abandoning his empty lab to run for office as a Democrat, although he returned this year. Some researchers gave up on Carolina: Abbey Hatcher, the public health professor, left U.N.C. and took her work elsewhere.

Dr. Bey, the epidemiologist, has remained. But she questions the rosy picture the university touts.

“What is success,” she asked, “when there are so many researchers who have lost their funding?”

A series examining disruption to research and discovery under Trump.

item.title: House Democrats Open Inquiry After Incoming Lawmaker Accused of Sexual Harassment
item.description:
House Democrats are investigating Brian Poindexter, a Democrat elected last week to represent a congressional district in northeastern Ohio, after he faced an accusation of sexual harassment.

In a statement on Friday, Julie Merz, the executive director of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said the organization had “hired an independent, third-party firm to investigate any instance of inappropriate behavior, conduct interviews and gather the facts.”

Ms. Merz said the committee, which is the House Democratic campaign arm, would have more to say after the investigation was completed.

The investigation follows an allegation that surfaced late in the race from a woman Mr. Poindexter’s campaign described as a “volunteer.” An advocacy organization for victims of sexual misconduct described the woman as a “low-level campaign staffer.” Neither the organization nor the D.C.C.C. has specified the nature of the allegation, and the woman has not been identified.

Mr. Poindexter defeated Representative Max Miller, a Republican whose ex-wife accused him of physically abusing her and their young daughter. Mr. Miller denied the accusations, which were a focal point in the campaign.

.

Asked about the allegation against Mr. Poindexter, his campaign said he “gave what he thought was an innocuous compliment to a volunteer.”

“He heard later that it made her feel uncomfortable and he felt awful,” the campaign said in a statement. “When Brian learned about this, we immediately began to work to get to the bottom of it with an outside H.R. firm. Neither Brian nor the campaign ever wants anyone to feel uncomfortable.”

The allegation against Mr. Poindexter was not made public before Election Day on Nov. 3. Democratic groups aligned with Mr. Poindexter said the woman had requested privacy.

Reckoning Action, the advocacy organization, said it is “providing support to” the woman who made the accusation against Mr. Poindexter, but declined to provide details about the allegation. The woman got in touch with Cheyenne Hunt, the group’s executive director, on Nov. 1, the group said.

Two political organizations that had endorsed Mr. Poindexter said in a statement on Friday that they had learned of the allegation toward the end of the campaign and are withdrawing their support while the investigation is conducted.

“We became aware of a report of alleged sexual harassment in the final days of the campaign. We informed the D.C.C.C. and connected the individual with legal advocacy and support services so she could determine how she wanted to proceed,” the two groups, the Blue Dog PAC, which supports moderates, and the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC, said in a joint statement.

The allegation prompted the groups to rescind their endorsements of Mr. Poindexter, the statement said, “pending the investigation being completed.” The groups had previously removed Mr. Poindexter’s name from their websites without providing a public explanation. The Blue Dog PAC had Mr. Poindexter’s name listed on its website as recently as Oct. 28, and the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC included him as recently as Nov. 1, according to internet archives.

“The individual requested that we did not disclose any details about this publicly because she did not want her identity becoming public and she wanted an opportunity to determine how she wanted to proceed while protecting herself,” the groups’ statement said. “We respected her desires, and also felt we needed to immediately pull our endorsements pending the investigation being completed.”

When asked about the matter on Friday, the House Democratic campaign arm said it had learned of the allegation in the “last several days leading up to the election,” and pointed to the comment from the PACs about the woman’s request.

Earlier this week, Mr. Poindexter told Politico that there was “nothing to read into” his removal from the websites of the two PACs.

“Just, I’m waiting to learn the political landscape,” he said.

Radio transmissions between active pilots and air traffic controllers at major airports offer a peek at how they navigated the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide ground stoppage on Friday.

An air traffic controller at Newark Liberty International Airport can be heard sharing the news with pilots.

Minutes later, at airports in Atlanta and Chicago, controllers said they had limited information.

As planes landed over the next hour and departures were stuck at their gates, air traffic controllers can be heard talking about significant gate issues and comparing the tarmac to a “parking lot.”

Amid the chaos, one pilot noted the date while talking to a Newark controller: “It’s not lost on me that it’s Friday the 13th.”

item.title: Ground Stop Scrambles Travel Plans for Sports Teams Across the Country
item.description:
Some professional and college sports teams were stuck on runways, or opting to pile into buses, ahead of games this weekend that are now uncertain due to the nationwide ground stop that was lifted Friday night.

Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of homeland security, said at a news conference on Friday that the ground stop was caused by technology upgrades “overwhelming” the flight communication system. Thousands of flights have been canceled, but no high-profile games have been affected so far, ahead of what is set to be a busy weekend in sports.

Dozens of teams had made it out of airports just ahead of the stop. But the N.B.A.’s Brooklyn Nets were not so lucky.

The Athletic reported that the Nets were stuck on a team plane on Friday. They have a game Saturday night against the Memphis Grizzles.

Also stuck at an airport was the University of Texas Longhorns football team, slated to play Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge, La., on Saturday night. Minutes before the stoppage, the Longhorns posted a video of players boarding a plane with the caption “Bayou bound.”

Both teams are in the Southeastern Conference, which said in a statement that it would work “to determine whether any adjustments to scheduled competitions become necessary.”

On Friday night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters that he encouraged college football teams to coordinate their flights with the Federal Aviation Administration “to make sure we have games going off tomorrow.”

While some teams, including the Longhorns, headed home from the airport to wait out the delay, a handful of others opted to travel the old-fashioned way: By bus.

The Athletic reported that among the longest drives was a 330-mile ride for the Purdue University Boilermakers, who are playing the University of Iowa Hawkeyes on Saturday night.

The University of Southern California women’s basketball team said they were grounded in Los Angeles ahead of a marquee game Sunday against the University of South Carolina Gamecocks, but were preparing to travel on Saturday.

In men’s college basketball, a Saturday game between University of North Carolina Greensboro and Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., was postponed because of the ground stop.

N.F.L. teams typically travel on Saturday for Sunday games. Five teams told The Athletic that their travel plans were not affected.

According to The Athletic, the stakes of the ground stop may be most significant for the National Women’s Soccer League, which is scheduled to hold its semifinals this weekend. The stop affected the Kansas City Current’s flight to New York City ahead of its game against Gotham FC on Sunday. The Utah Royals, playing the Washington Spirit on Saturday, traveled before the stoppage.

The N.B.A.’s Cleveland Cavaliers had planned to catch a flight home after their Friday night game in Miami. Kenny Atkinson, the Cavaliers head coach, told reporters before the game that he didn’t know if the team would make their flight.

“I think we’re scrambling to find hotel rooms in case,” Mr. Atkinson said, adding: “If not, we’ll sleep on the bus.”

item.title: Pilots and Controllers Kept Communicating During Outage
item.description:
A communications outage on Friday led the Federal Aviation Administration to pause departing flights nationwide, but pilots were not entirely cut off from federal air traffic controllers.

In a Friday night news conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage was intermittent, so federal controllers were still able to reach pilots.

“It wasn’t a complete blackout in communication or radar,” he said. “So we were able to keep some of those communications going.”

But even in a complete outage, aviation authorities have multiple backups to maintain contact with pilots.

Pilots and air traffic controllers primarily communicate by voice radio, using primary, backup and emergency frequencies.

Controllers and airline dispatchers can also send text-based messages to pilots. And many commercial planes are equipped with satellite communications, which are especially useful for reaching people on the ground when the planes are flying in remote airspace like over the ocean.

If a control tower loses radio capabilities, it can also communicate with pilots with high-intensity colored lights, which pilots can acknowledge by rocking their wings or flashing lights in response.

item.title: Even High-Flying Democrats Found Themselves Grounded in the Mile High City
item.description:
Pete Buttigieg could not believe what he had just watched. The former transportation secretary stood at the corner of the hotel bar in Denver, where CNN had just finished broadcasting the Trump administration’s news conference about the ground stop that stopped flights nationwide on Friday.

Mr. Buttigieg was among the thousands of Democrats who had gathered in Denver this week for a conference designed to chart the party’s future and celebrate their midterm wins. The ground stop stranded some of the party’s top rising stars and their staffs.

People accustomed to having inside information suddenly had very little.

At a table to Mr. Buttigieg’s left sat Gov. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, Gov. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan. They munched on Parmesan fries and checked their phones as they waited for news of their flights.

To his right, Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia scanned his Senate group chats to check for updates from secure channels and Senator Mark Warner of Virginia.

But Mr. Buttigieg, glancing up at the television, struggled to comprehend the performance of his successor, Secretary Sean Duffy.

“You can just write down the comic book asterisk swearing characters,” Mr. Buttigieg said when a New York Times reporter asked for his impressions of the news conference. “I have questions.”

The downtown hotel bar resembled the famous bar scene in “Star Wars.” The stranded politicians bemoaned the lack of information from the federal government and their inability to get home.

One New England-based operative booked a rental car and planned to drive back to Boston. Others looked up how many hours it would take to get to the East Coast on Amtrak. (The answer: more than 40.) Aides to one prominent Democratic governor, who had flown to Denver on a private jet, fielded questions from others in the bar about whether they could hitch a ride home.

A few people working for Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois — who did not come to Denver — commandeered a long table where Anne Caprara, his chief of staff, worked two phones as she juggled rumors, emergencies back home and calls from the boss. She said Mr. Pritzker was furious about the lack of information coming from the Trump administration.

“Welcome to Denver’s hottest bar, the Mos Eisley Cantina of politics,” Ms. Caprara said, referring to the “Star Wars” bar. “With ‘Veep’ characters and a ‘Terminator 2’ vibe.”

Shane Goldmacher contributed reporting.

item.title: What to Know About Friday’s Nationwide Ground Stop
item.description:
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, after outdated air traffic communications equipment became overloaded with data and began to fail, officials said.

The outage stranded thousands of passengers and caused widespread delays from which airlines and airports are still struggling to recover. It also highlighted persistent vulnerabilities in the aging U.S. air traffic infrastructure and a funding fight, as administration officials demanded lawmakers approve tens of billions of dollars more to accelerate systemwide upgrades.

Here’s what to know.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, told reporters at the White House Friday night that the radar and other air traffic communications started to falter at 3:36 p.m. when old routers became overloaded with data. While the failures were not universal, they were pervasive enough to prompt officials to issue the unusual nationwide moratorium on takeoffs, Mr. Duffy said.

Appearing alongside him at the White House, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, stressed that there was no evidence that nefarious activity had triggered the technology failures.

“We’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack,” Mr. Mullin said, suggesting that new equipment and new technology the Mr. Duffy’s department had added to the old infrastructure was what had overwhelmed it.

Mr. Duffy insisted that the failure was caused by the antiquated, legacy communications equipment, not recent upgrades to the system.

“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Mr. Duffy said, predicting that until significant upgrades are made, “it’s going to continue to fail.”

Mr. Duffy warned that it would take “some time” for air travel nationwide to recover from the ground stop, predicting flight schedules would be fully back to normal by the time the Thanksgiving travel season begins.

“I believe that it’s going to take us some time to get back to capacity,” he said, adding: “We’re going to have some makeup to do.”

Mr. Duffy said that the F.A.A. would prioritize larger commercial flights ahead of private and charter flights, to get previously grounded flights off the ground.

Mr. Duffy has long been pushing for a sweeping overhaul of the U.S. air traffic infrastructure, routinely complaining that controllers have been hampered by the country’s failure to upgrade outdated equipment.

“We have old, old switches, old routers — we use 1980s little copper lines,” he said to reporters Friday. Only last week, the F.A.A. announced that it had begun to phase out the use of floppy disks.

Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion to fund upgrades to the country’s aging air traffic facilities and networks, some of which has been directed toward communications system upgrades. Mr. Duffy noted Friday that air traffic facilities that had been upgraded to digital systems did not experience the same overloading issues that prompted the F.A.A. to issue the ground stop order.

But he stressed that having an air traffic control system dependent on a “patchwork” of upgrades and fixes was untenable, calling on Congress to spend tens of billions more to allow for more upgrades.

For months, Mr. Duffy has been calling on the Republican-controlled Congress to give his department another $30 billion to accelerate efforts to upgrade air traffic control systems. On Friday night, he upped the ante, telling reporters he wanted $50 billion — and that he wanted it before the end of the year.

“This is an emergency, I want Congress to give us emergency funding,” he said, adding: “How many more times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?”

But it is unclear whether Republicans will prioritize such a sum before the end of the year, after which control of Congress shifts to the Democrats, who are expected to scrutinize how the F.A.A. has utilized air traffic funding they have received so far. Republican lawmakers have filed bills in the House and Senate to authorize $30 billion in air traffic upgrades, but neither piece of legislation has cosponsors.

Later on Friday, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House’s top-ranking Democrat, appeared to reject Mr. Duffy’s accusing tone and shifted the blame back to the Trump administration.

“Today’s unprecedented breakdown is the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents under the Trump administration’s failed leadership,” he said in a statement, adding that “American travelers deserve timely answers from the Trump administration about how and why this happened and assurances that steps are being taken to ensure that our air travel system remains safe and functional.”

item.title: A Democrat Wins the Alaska Governor’s Race for the First Time Since 1998
item.description:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, an energetic former state lawmaker who ran as a pragmatic coalition-builder, will be Alaska’s next governor, The Associated Press said. He will be the first Democrat elected to lead the state since 1998 and the youngest governor in state history.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, defeated Bernadette Wilson, a former Republican talk show host who owns a garbage-collection company.

In his victory declaration, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins said that Alaskans had “voted for change.”

“Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska,” he added.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins is a former ultramarathoner and mountaineer from Sitka who dropped out of Yale to win his first legislative seat at age 23, and then spent a decade building bipartisan coalitions and sounding alarms about the state’s precarious finances.

He visited all 19 of Alaska’s boroughs during his campaign, making promises to rebuild public education and the state’s ferry system, lower the cost of housing and energy, and protect Alaskan fisheries. He also pledged to put Alaska’s finances on a more sustainable footing. That might mean he has to persuade the Legislature to find new revenue sources in an oil-rich state that has no personal income tax or statewide sales tax and has struggled in recent years to fund basic public services while also paying an annual dividend to residents from Alaska’s oil revenues.

“I am the pro-math candidate,” he said at one debate.

Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins won in a state where Democrats make up just 11 percent of the electorate with a campaign built to appeal to moderates and Republicans tired of legislative gridlock in the capital, Juneau. In the final stretch of the campaign, he touted endorsements from a string of Republicans and pledged to appoint a politically balanced transition team and cabinet. He has also promised to live in Juneau, a sore point among some Alaskans tired of governors who essentially commute to the capital from more accessible and urbanized Anchorage.

Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a conservative Republican barred by term limits from seeking another four years, has clashed repeatedly with the bipartisan coalition that runs the Legislature, a coalition that Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins helped build and lead in his time in the Statehouse.

Over the last two years, Mr. Dunleavy vetoed 31 pieces of legislation, including proposals to restore pensions for public employees and teachers, establish a retirement savings program for private-sector workers, impose new taxes on e-cigarettes and modernize the state’s corporate tax system.

In an interview last month, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins said he would start his work as governor by addressing unfinished business, including bills passed by the Legislature but killed by Mr. Dunleavy. When he takes office on Dec. 7, Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins will enjoy a short-term budget surplus thanks to the war in Iran, which sent oil prices skyward. But big decisions still loom about how to ensure long-term financial stability given the state’s reliance on the oil and gas industry.

“The state is too fragile already,” he said. “Alaska is paying the price of uncertainty, and this is just something we need to get done.”

Ms. Wilson, who finished second in the four-person race, campaigned on a promise to restore full dividend payments from the oil-revenue account known as the Permanent Fund, which comes from levies from the state’s oil and gas production. She also said she would take a tougher approach with Republican lawmakers who work across party lines.

She referred to Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins, known as J.K.T. in Alaska political circles and in campaign materials, as “Just Keep Taxing.”

But Republican infighting helped Mr. Kreiss-Tomkins win a majority of votes even before Alaska’s ranked-choice process kicked in: The other two Republicans in the four-person field refused Ms. Wilson’s calls to exit the race, prompting internal sniping. President Trump, who carried Alaska in all three campaigns, endorsed Ms. Wilson. But in a year of Democratic triumphs, the president’s backing didn’t provide the boost Republicans expected.

item.title: Mary Peltola’s Lead Widens as Alaska Senate Vote Count Continues
item.description:
Mary Peltola, a Democrat, widened her lead over Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, in the latest vote tally in Alaska’s Senate race, but the election remained uncalled on Friday as the count continued.

If neither candidate wins an outright majority, the race will be decided next week by ranked-choice tabulation.

Ms. Peltola had 49.8 percent of the vote and led Mr. Sullivan by nearly four percentage points in incomplete results as of Friday night. She is on track to eventually prevail, according to a New York Times analysis.

The race between Mr. Sullivan, a two-term incumbent, and Ms. Peltola, a former congresswoman, is the only Senate battle still uncalled in a midterm cycle that featured sweeping Democratic victories.

A spokesman for Mr. Sullivan, Nate Adams, said on Friday night after the latest release of results: “We’re still waiting for every ballot to be counted. And we’ll see what happens from there.”

The delay in Alaska is in part because of the time the state allows for mail ballots to be received and counted and in part because of the state’s unique ranked-choice system. Mr. Sullivan and Ms. Peltola faced two other candidates after emerging from a nonpartisan primary in August.

In Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system, voters can rank the candidates on the ballot in order of preference. If no candidate gets over 50 percent of the first-choice votes, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and their supporters’ second-choice votes are counted. The tabulation continues until two candidates are left; the candidate with more votes wins.

In Alaska, Ms. Peltola and Mr. Sullivan contended with Gerald L. Heikes, a Republican, and Dan J. Sullivan, an unaffiliated candidate with a similar name to the Republican senator. Mr. Heikes and Dan J. Sullivan have combined to win about 4 percent of the vote so far.

Democrats had recruited Mr. Heikes and Dan J. Sullivan onto the ballot in an effort to dilute Senator Sullivan’s vote share. The Times analysis found that among voters who picked Dan J. Sullivan as their first choice, more selected Ms. Peltola as their second choice than picked Senator Sullivan.

Ms. Peltola, a centrist whose campaign slogan was “fish, family and freedom,” would be the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate. She would also be the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska in nearly two decades.

Democrats, riding widespread voter frustration with high prices in President Trump’s second term, have won 55 Senate seats in the midterms, securing the largest majority held by either party since President Barack Obama’s first term.

The president’s war in Iran and his tariff fight with Canada adversely affected Alaska, where voters faced particularly high gasoline prices. Senator Sullivan decided to campaign with Mr. Trump, despite the president’s poor approval ratings, in a bid to activate conservative Republican voters.

Mr. Trump won Alaska by about 14 percentage points in 2024, but the state has been gradually shifting left in presidential elections over the last quarter-century.

If Ms. Peltola were to win the Senate race, it would give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber, more than they have captured in any election since Mr. Obama won the presidency in 2008.

item.title: Bomb Found at Ethanol Plant in Peoria, Ill., Mayor Says
item.description:
Parts of Peoria and East Peoria, neighboring cities in Illinois, were evacuated on Friday night after what a city official described as a bomb was found in an industrial area along the riverfront.

Mayor Rita Ali of Peoria, a city of 110,000 residents, said emergency workers had discovered a bomb at the BioUrja ethanol plant, and that a one-mile radius around that facility was evacuated on both sides of the Illinois River, which separates the two cities.

The Peoria police chief, Brad Dixon, said early Saturday that “bomb technicians rendered the package safe” on Friday night, but that a search of the facility was continuing and that the evacuation order remained in effect. He declined to comment on whether there were suspects.

In a separate news conference, Ms. Ali said that “we don’t know whether there’s one device or whether there’s multiple devices.” She described it as “a real crisis situation right now.”

For hours on Friday evening, parts of Peoria and East Peoria were shut down as city, state and federal officials swarmed the ethanol plant. For much of that time, the emergency had been described only as a bomb threat, not a verified bomb.

It was not immediately clear how many people lived in the evacuation zone, which included commercial and residential areas.

Officials from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives were at the scene, and Illinois state troopers blocked traffic in the area. Jon Pardi, the country singer, canceled a concert in Peoria that had been scheduled for Friday, citing “an active local safety concern.”

State and federal officials, including Gov. JB Pritzker and Representative Darin LaHood, posted on social media that they were monitoring the situation and urged residents to heed evacuation orders. Ms. Ali told Peoria residents that they could take shelter in the basement of a local high school.

Chief Dixon said the ethanol plant received a bomb threat on Friday, and that officials located a suspicious package around 2 p.m. Several hours later, he said, “the package was deemed a credible threat” and “a blast radius was determined at one mile.” Hours after that, he said, the device was rendered safe.

He said emergency crews would continue to search the plant, a process that would likely go on for several hours. Peoria officials planned to provide more information around midday Saturday. Attempts to reach officials with BioUrja were not immediately successful.

Though bomb threats and brief evacuations are relatively common in the United States, it is far more rare for officials to find an explosive device that could pose a large-scale safety threat.

“Nationally, when a bomb threat comes in, typically, it’s not legitimate and they’re doing it to cause an evacuation of a building or something like that,” Chief Dixon said. “This is not the case here. We found a credible package that we deem to be a threat.”
