item.title: Ex-Convict? Come Live With Memi and Scott.
item.description:
The sprawling yellow house with the red trim has an air hockey table in the living room and framed Christmas photos on the walls. With five bedrooms, an airy kitchen and a lemon tree in the backyard, the home in Oakland, Calif., is perfect for a large family.

Or several convicts just released from prison.

Over the past three years, a rotation of recently released inmates, many of them convicted of murder, has cycled through the home of Surmiche Vaughn, 42, and her husband, Scott Patterson, 47. The houseguests are part of a program run by an Oakland nonprofit trying to keep former prisoners off the street.

Overall, 24 men have stayed with the couple, usually five or so at a time.

In return for hosting the men, Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Patterson receive about $1,500 per tenant per month, payments that are covered by the nonprofit, Impact Justice.

The experimental initiative is one of the few of its kind in the nation. It operates in the Bay Area and Los Angeles, and all of its participants are coming off prison sentences of 10 years or longer, most commonly for murder, but also for attempted murder, manslaughter and robbery. Some 130 hosts have taken in prisoners since the program started in 2018.

Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Patterson know that their decision has raised eyebrows, even among loved ones.

“At first our friends were like, ‘You’re doing what? Girl, what?’” said Ms. Vaughn, who goes by Memi.

Having ex-convicts in the community has caused some anxiety among the neighbors. Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Patterson admit that they were initially apprehensive as well. What if it invited disruption or violence into their home?

One of Ms. Vaughn’s 21-year-old twin daughters at first avoided staying at the house when she visited from college, Ms. Vaughn said. She came around about a year ago, and now invites her friends over.

But Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Patterson say that hosting the men has largely gone off without a hitch.

Years in prison have taught the former convicts to be on good behavior so as not to risk a return, said Ms. Vaughn, who owns and runs a massage therapy business in Oakland. The house is quieter and cleaner than when her twins were still living at home, she said with a chuckle, and the rent money goes straight toward the children’s college tuition.

The men mostly just want a chance to move forward, said Mr. Patterson, who works as a hospital X-ray technician.

“They’re not going to do anything to compromise that,” he said.

Philippe Kelly, 43, spent more than two decades in prison for a fatal shooting he committed when he was a teenager. He moved in with Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Patterson in 2023.

He said it was a tough adjustment back to the real world after so many years in an environment that “disconnects you from society, it disconnects you from relationships, and it disconnects you from your humanity.”

Mr. Kelly, who now works as an organizer at a nonprofit promoting civil rights and criminal justice reform, said Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Patterson had treated him like a friend and let him adjust on his own timeline.

“There’s a lot to be said about folks who open their home up to strangers and allow them the opportunity to reacclimate into society without any pressure, without any judgment, and just with open arms and love,” he said.

There are occasional problems within the program, known as the Homecoming Project. Sometimes participants don’t get along with their hosts, or break house rules, such as curfews, quiet hours and bans on alcohol and smoking. Impact Justice will occasionally relocate participants to homes that would be a better fit, and in rare cases have discharged people from the program, said Bernadette Butler, who leads the program for Impact Justice.

To match released prisoners with hosts, Impact Justice, which is funded by state grants as well as several family foundations, gets referrals from probation and parole officers and then screens and interviews potential candidates. They are looking for people who want to transform their lives. Anyone convicted of sex crimes is excluded.

In California, people are typically released from prison with $200. During those early days, they’re highly susceptible to falling back into old ways, becoming homeless or using drugs, said Reuben Jonathan Miller, a sociologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies incarceration.

Having a safe place to land and the care of people who don’t treat them as criminals can be transformative, he said.

Impact Justice pays for tenants to live with families for six months, and the recidivism rate for the program’s roughly 290 participants in that time is zero, the organization said. Most participants finish their home stay with full-time employment.

Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Patterson for the most part haven’t told their neighbors about their houseguests, saying they think the men should be free to share their pasts on their own terms. Some neighbors were not pleased to learn about the program from a reporter.

Yuhna Del Rosario, 32, who rents the home next door, said it made her nervous. “Oh, hell no,” she said. “They’re very brave.”

A few doors down, Leticia Rivera, 69, initially expressed similar unease. Crime had decreased in the neighborhood since she moved there in the 1990s, she said, and she bristled at anything that could threaten that.

She was quiet for a few minutes as she watered the tomatoes and squash plants in her front yard, and then acknowledged that there hadn’t been any problems for the neighborhood thus far, so maybe it was OK after all.

“Everybody deserves a second chance,” Ms. Rivera said.

Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Patterson began accepting tenants from Impact Justice in 2023 after encouragement from Ms. Vaughn’s father, Surville Vaughn, who had hosted tenants in his three-bedroom apartment, also in east Oakland.

Mr. Vaughn, 76, has hosted more released prisoners than any other homeowner in the program. He said he hadn’t had issues with tenants stealing or doing drugs. Sometimes there are minor problems, he said, like when a tenant is playing music too loudly, but all have been easily remedied.

The program focuses on people who’ve completed long sentences because they are often most disconnected from their loved ones, and also tend to have lower recidivism rates. One recent tenant of Ms. Vaughn’s had recently completed a 43-year sentence.

It takes some time for the men to adjust. On his first night, one tenant fell asleep still wearing his boots and backpack with the door to his bedroom open.

When Ms. Vaughn talked with him the next morning, he said that he wasn’t accustomed to having privacy after so many years of not having any. He also said he was uncomfortable in a bedroom that felt so much larger than a prison cell. He soon moved into the home’s smallest bedroom, which felt more familiar.

Ms. Vaughn said that was the first time she was home alone with a tenant — her husband was out of town — and one of only two times she has felt some anxiety.

The second occurred when she learned two men from rival L.A. gangs would be living in her house. “Then I was surprised because they were the ones that got along the most,” she said, adding that they had ended up bonding over shared experiences and what had happened decades ago. “A lot of that stuff is behind them.”

Helping the men with this major transition and learning about their struggles have made the couple’s own problems feel quotidian, Ms. Vaughn said.

“They’ve shaped me to be a better partner to my husband, a better person,” she said. “I’m able to stop and smell the roses.”

They try to make the tenants feel normal and included in their lives. Mr. Patterson plays video games and watches basketball with some of the tenants, and listens to tales of their pasts. Ms. Vaughn takes them grocery shopping and gives them advice about women.

The men cook and clean for themselves. But every Thanksgiving, Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Patterson hosts a lunch in which they invite their family and friends, as well as all former and current tenants.

Mr. Kelly has since moved out, but he calls the couple once a week to check in. Mr. Patterson said he felt like a “proud parent” the first time that Mr. Kelly excitedly FaceTimed them from his new apartment.

Frank Dryden, 50, was released from prison last year after serving 13 years for shooting two people in a robbery. He said living with Ms. Vaughn and Mr. Patterson helped him stick to a commitment he made to himself while he was in prison: to stay out of trouble.

He has gotten a job with the state picking up trash on the side of the highway, and started volunteering with a local church to deliver food to needy people.

“Either that or go back out here on the streets and hang out with the people I used to hang out with, and do what I used to do,” he said.

Jesse Barron contributed reporting, and Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: Top Democrat Eyes Filibuster-Proof Bill to Unlock Affordability Agenda
item.description:
A top House Democrat mapping out how to leverage his party’s vast majorities in Congress next year to push through a sweeping economic agenda is considering using a filibuster-proof bill to muscle it through both chambers and to President Trump’s desk.

The approach, outlined by Representative Brendan Boyle, the Pennsylvania Democrat in line to be chairman of the House Budget Committee in January, would be one way of forcing Mr. Trump to either embrace or veto broadly popular measures to lower living costs.

Triumphant after electoral victories delivered them more than 255 seats in the House and at least 55 seats in the Senate, Democrats are weighing the best strategy for quickly delivering the affordability agenda they promised voters, including tackling the soaring costs of health care, child care and housing.

Mr. Boyle, the 49-year-old son of a janitor for Pennsylvania’s transportation authority and a school crossing guard, is now positioned to lead the way from his perch at the helm of the House panel that handles budget matters and sets spending priorities.

In an interview, Mr. Boyle said it was “worth exploring” using budget reconciliation — a tool that allows the party in power to bypass opposition from the minority and push through fiscal legislation on majority votes — to unlock the affordability agenda Democrats ran on, including reversing Medicaid cuts Republicans enacted unilaterally in 2025.

“I think any time we can pass good, popular, meaningful legislation, that only strengthens our hand in any ultimate negotiation with the White House,” Mr. Boyle said.

He also said he would like Democrats to forge a deal with Mr. Trump on the statutory limit on the national debt, ending what has become a perennial cycle of high-stakes fiscal clashes between the president and Congress that have repeatedly brought the country dangerously close to a federal default. Mr. Boyle has long pushed for legislation that would allow the Treasury Department to suspend the debt limit, subject to congressional override, rather than requiring an affirmative vote by Congress to increase it.

“He wants it raised,” he said of Mr. Trump. “We never again want to see a Democratic president have to have this held like a gun against their head, the same way it happened to Joe Biden and to Barack Obama.”

A sharp but sociable communicator, Mr. Boyle is part of a younger vanguard of House Democrats rising to the top echelons of the party. He said that no final decisions had been made, but outlined a scenario in which Democrats early next year would first try to pass their economic agenda with some Republican backing, which they would need to steer around a filibuster in the Senate. He suggested Democrats could then move to a partisan reconciliation package if they failed to win over G.O.P. supporters.

“It’s worth exploring reconciliation now that we have both the House and the Senate; however, I think it’s also worth exploring the fact that we’re 56,” Mr. Boyle said, referring to the number of Senate seats Democrats would control if they won a seat in Alaska, where their candidate was leading. “Are there four Senate Republicans who we could work with on issue X, on issue Y, to get things passed in a more expeditious manner?”

That strategy would be in step with what Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, has privately outlined to his caucus. He has said he is prepared to move to a filibuster-proof effort if Republicans will not back Democratic legislation meant to address cost-of-living issues.

Mr. Boyle said he would defer to Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader who is expected to become speaker, on whether the costs of an economic package would need to be offset by new taxes.

Democrats could try to pay for the cost of such a plan by rolling back tax cuts for the “megawealthy” that Republicans enacted during the first and second Trump administrations, he said.

Or they could not pay for them at all. Mr. Boyle said Democrats could argue: “Look, those folks passed a massive, $5 trillion bill and only paid for a fraction of it; we certainly shouldn’t be held to a different standard.”

In 2021, when Democrats used their governing trifecta in Congress under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. to advance a legislative package through reconciliation, feuding broke out between the moderate and progressive flanks of the party over the scope and cost of the bill.

The House eventually passed a $2.2 trillion measure known as “Build Back Better.” But in the months of debate, centrists in the Senate pushed to narrow the measure substantially, outraging progressives, who then threatened to withhold their support for a separate $1 trillion bipartisan infrastructure bill.

Not yet at the helm of the budget panel, Mr. Boyle still vividly remembers the internal party churn that threatened to tank both bills and the multiday slogs he endured to pass them out of committee.

“When it got to the Senate, because of the math of 50-50, where every Senate Democrat could be king or queen, the bill got slimmed down considerably, about half of the size,” he said. “The name changed, and a lot of the things that I felt the best about in that bill were stripped out.”

“The biggest difference now,” Mr. Boyle said, “is 56 is a lot easier than 50.”

Michael Gold contributed reporting.

item.title: ‘Democrat’ in Alaska’s House Race Is Doing Time in a New York Prison
item.description:
In the midterm election’s closing days, the phones of left-leaning Alaskans pinged with texts urging them to back Eric Hafner, the lone Democrat on the four-person ballot for a U.S. House seat.

But Democratic Party leaders in Alaska and Washington were actually backing an independent on the ballot, Bill Hill, and for good reason: Mr. Hafner is a felon serving a 20-year sentence in a federal prison in Otisville, N.Y., about 4,351 miles from Anchorage.

Who paid for those text messages is of particular interest in Alaska, where purportedly dirty tricks by Democratic operatives put an alternative Dan Sullivan on the Senate ballot against the incumbent Republican, Senator Dan Sullivan.

Mr. Hafner’s unknown benefactor was likely hoping to confuse voters and aid the Republican incumbent, Representative Nick Begich. Democrats point to the texts as proof that nobody’s hands are clean in Alaska.

Mr. Hafner and his chief supporter — his mother — say the motive doesn’t matter, even as the mysterious outside help has elevated his jailhouse bid into a potential spoiler.

“Why should we care where they came from?” Ms. Hafner asked.

Official results may not come for days in the races for Alaska’s Senate seat and its lone House seat. The winners will likely be determined after officials tabulate second- and third-place choices on the state’s ranked-choice ballots.

In the House contest, Mr. Begich, the scion of an Alaska political dynasty, holds 48.5 percent of counted votes, and Mr. Hill, 41.2 percent. Mr. Hafner, who has never visited Alaska, has nearly 8 percent.

“This guy may actually matter,” Eric Croft, the state Democratic Party chairman, said.

If enough supporters of Mr. Hafner and the fourth candidate, the Libertarian Jim McDermott, ranked Mr. Hill ahead of Mr. Begich, the independent could still win. But preliminary ballot data suggest that Mr. Hill faces an uphill battle. Only about 45 percent of Mr. Hafner’s votes would ultimately transfer to Mr. Hill, while nearly half would be exhausted because voters did not rank either of the two leading candidates.

Carol Gray, a University of Alaska Fairbanks political scientist, said most of Mr. Hafner’s votes — “maybe all of them” — came from Alaskans angry at Republicans and backing any Democrat on the ballot. Mr. Hill’s decision not to run as a Democrat — no decision at all for the lifelong independent, according to his team — may prove to be his campaign’s undoing.

Mr. Croft was not so sure. Eight percent for someone like Mr. Hafner? “That just feels too hard to believe,” he said. “That becomes a dirty trick that worked.”

Mr. Begich has denied any involvement by his campaign to boost Mr. Hafner. The only clear Republican fingerprints on the caper are actually on the similar electoral efforts of Mr. Hafner’s mother.

“We’re a politically engaged family,” she said.

She ran as a Democrat in Alaska’s nonpartisan U.S. Senate primary, backed by $346,000 in ads from Fair Deal Alaska, a super PAC funded almost entirely by committees tied to Senate Republicans and the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan. Ms. Hafner won less than 1 percent of the primary vote and failed to advance.

She finished third in Alaska’s Democratic House primary in 2018 and second in Wyoming’s Democratic primary two years later.

Ms. Hafner and her son both use a South Dakota mail-forwarding service as their campaign addresses. She said Republicans did not recruit either of them, denied any connection to the Republican-bought ads and described both her and her son’s politics as “progressive through and through.”

Still, Mr. Hafner’s handwritten filing for a Florida U.S. House special election last year listed ancillary committees including “MAGA Republicans Victory Fund,” “Secure the Border Florida” and “America First Florida Always.” His entry in Alaska’s official voter guide this year called on voters to unite against short-term greed.

Ballot stacking — essentially, recruiting candidates to siphon votes and split the opposition — is a time-honored tradition in Alaska and other states with low hurdles to run for office.

In Mr. Hafner’s case, Mr. Begich’s allies appear to have capitalized on a history of quixotic campaigns dating back to 2016, when “the Rev. Dr. Eric Hafner” finished second in the Republican primary for Hawaii’s 2nd Congressional District.

Two years later, Mr. Hafner ran as a Democrat for a U.S. House seat in Oregon, another place he had never lived, telling a reporter that Portland’s live-and-let-live vibe — especially on marijuana — matched his own.

Mr. Hafner, who his mother says “runs to win,” has plenty of time for politics.

Between 2016 and 2018, according to court records, Mr. Hafner threatened to kill lawyers, police officers and judges in Monmouth County, N.J., tied to his past juvenile and family court cases. He pleaded guilty in 2022 to two counts of making interstate threats and one count of making false bomb threats and received a 20-year prison sentence.

In 2024, Mr. Hafner paid the $100 fee to run for Alaska’s U.S. House seat from prison. He won fewer than 500 primary votes, but reached the general election after several Republicans ahead of him dropped out to aid Mr. Begich.

Alaska Democrats, worried about confusing voters and hurting the Democratic incumbent, Mary Peltola, sued to block his candidacy. Republicans fought to keep him on the ballot and won. But Mr. Hafner’s 3,417 votes — one percent of the total — were not decisive in Ms. Peltola’s loss.

This year, Democrats lacked a big-name contender for the House seat after an Anchorage pastor, Matt Schultz, dropped out. So they backed Mr. Hill, a commercial fisherman and former teacher and school administrator.

Mr. Hafner filed on May 10 via another handwritten form mailed from his cell. This time, fearing voter confusion, independent groups spent nearly $500,000 urging people not to rank him. Online and radio spots said the “D” next to Mr. Hafner’s name stood for “doing time.”

At the same time, thousands of Alaskans received text messages supporting Mr. Hafner. The messages accused Mr. Hill of being a closet conservative and noting that Mr. Hafner supported “Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, and will fight back against Trump and his enablers.”

The texts did not include any detail about who sent them, which may violate federal election law, depending on how many went out and how they were sent. So far, no outside group has reported spending money supporting Mr. Hafner.

Ms. Hafner doesn’t care who paid for the messages. She’s just grateful.

“If something lands in your lap, you’re not going to say ‘no thanks,’” she said.

Mr. Hafner is already barred from serving, because the Constitution requires U.S. House members to live in the state they represent when elected.

His mother sees a path around that: “Somebody needs to tell President Trump that Eric has earned a pardon,” she said.

item.title: As Congress Plans Investigations, White House Prepares Ferocious Response
item.description:
In his first term, President Trump approached congressional investigations with a strategy of resisting and stonewalling, hoping to stall the inquiries until Democrats ran out of time.

But in anticipation of Democrats’ return to control of Congress in his second term, Mr. Trump has embarked on an even more aggressive maneuver: threatening to treat some legislative oversight as a potential crime.

That tactic is expected to be part of an all-out effort by the White House to block Democratic congressional oversight over the next two years.

The pushback will be led in part by Mr. Trump’s new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, a political brawler with extensive experience on Capitol Hill. It will be bolstered by a Justice Department and a White House Counsel’s Office that have been quietly laying the groundwork for the fight.

At stake: whether the Trump administration can prevent Democrats from getting access to its decision-making and scrutinizing the actions of top officials and powerful people, in and out of government. Mr. Trump has also become increasingly concerned that some of his biggest supporters who give money toward his prized construction projects will be targeted, according to aides and his public statements.

The White House is bracing for a spate of investigations, and officials say they are ready to punch back.

“If you’re not ready for these fights, you’re going to be in a whole lot of trouble legally and politically,” said Hogan Gidley, a White House deputy press secretary in the first Trump administration. “They have a really good plan and have a good leader at the top in Stephen Miller. He is primed and ready for this fight, like no one else would be.”

While clashes between lawmakers and the White House over congressional investigations are not unusual, the escalating threats could result in a remarkable battle that reshapes the balance of power between the two branches of government. Legal experts have said the White House’s contention that congressional investigations “may cross the line into blatant criminality” pushes the bounds of the law, but much remains unclear about how the courts might handle the coming fights.

“As the president has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hard-working Americans,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”

Top Democrats have shown no indications they are intimidated or plan to slow down. They have already sent letters to scores of potential targets of investigations, on everything from cuts to scientific research to donors for Mr. Trump’s White House ballroom.

On Thursday, Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Representative Robert Garcia of California and Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut announced an investigation into a top Trump fund-raiser, Meredith O’Rourke, after reports indicated that she coordinated more than $800 million in contributions to the president’s favorite construction projects.

“The fund-raising operation that President Trump reportedly directs with your assistance reeks of potential corruption and the potential for quid pro quo politics,” the lawmakers wrote to Ms. O’Rourke.

A spokesman for Ms. O’Rourke said that Mr. Trump could not be bought, and that Democrats’ accusations were baseless.

The White House plan to shield Mr. Trump’s donors and threaten Democrats has been taking shape for months in response to what they believe will be an unrelenting pace of oversight.

The Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel over the summer quietly published an opinion asserting that even communications by those outside government could be covered by executive privilege if they concerned Mr. Trump and his top aides.

Rachel Jag, a former staff member to Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio, the newly elected Republican leader in the House, will coordinate the department’s response to Democratic subpoenas, records requests and accusations. She is overseeing a large staff, but the department is seeking experienced lawyers to fill out what are expected to be high-workload jobs.

The department has been hit by a wave of departures, and Ms. Jag took over the role on an interim basis after Patrick Davis, who served as the department’s head of legislative affairs, quit just before the midterm elections for reasons that remain unclear.

At the White House, Mr. Trump appointed Mr. Miller chief of staff after Democrats swept to victory last week.

“Stephen Miller is President Trump’s wartime general,” said Mike Davis, a former chief counsel for nominations on the Senate Judiciary Committee. “He’s very experienced, including on the Hill.”

And the White House Counsel’s Office began beefing up its staff, hiring two lawyers to deal with oversight.

On Saturday, the president posted on social media: “Threatening letters have been sent to many people, all innocent, from Democrat Political Leaders. By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Top lawyers across the federal government snapped into action.

Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, sent a letter to Mr. Blumenthal on Wednesday, warning of “significant legal consequences” should he continue to pursue an investigation into the ballroom donors.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that top leaders at the Justice Department had been working with Mr. Reitz.

At a news conference, Mr. Blanche said there were “no ongoing criminal investigations” into statements made by incoming members of Congress. Nevertheless, he said, Justice Department officials were concerned about some of the statements made after the election.

“There can come a point when a criticism becomes a threat,” Mr. Blanche said, adding, “There are threats, which can be allowed as well, but at some point it does become a crime.”

Then, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, put Mr. Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, on notice that he could be committing criminal acts by pursuing investigations.

Asked about his letter to Mr. Garcia and whether it meant the White House was prepared to prosecute lawmakers, Mr. Scharf said that “the letter stands for itself.”

“I meant everything I said,” Mr. Scharf added in an interview on Thursday. He declined to address how the administration’s efforts squared with the “speech or debate” clause of the Constitution, which shields lawmakers from being subpoenaed or prosecuted by the executive branch over their legislative work.

Congress, at its core, is a legislative body, not a prosecutorial one. To the extent Congress has investigative powers, they are to obtain information to help in the act of legislating.

If administration officials fight congressional subpoenas, federal courts would have to referee — litigation that could take months or years to resolve.

Mr. Scharf and others are collecting examples of lawmakers who they say are making clear their investigations have no legislative purpose.

Donald F. McGahn II, the White House counsel for part of Mr. Trump’s first term, said the White House had long prepared for the oversight.

“They’ve talked to a lot of people who’ve done it before,” he said.

Of Mr. Scharf’s letter, Mr. McGahn said, “It’s smart to chronicle in writing all of the things that the various Democratic congressmen will say about oversight that shows that they’re not doing it for a legislative purpose.”

Stanley M. Brand, the top lawyer in the House under Speaker Thomas P. (Tip) O’Neill Jr., said the White House threats against lawmakers carried little legal power. But he said Congress would have difficulty enforcing any subpoena should the administration refuse to comply, because any criminal referral would go to the Justice Department. And the attorney general reports to Mr. Trump.

“Although the Democrats control the Congress, the administration still controls the Department of Justice, and so to the extent that people get referred for contempt under the criminal statute, I don’t expect that to go anywhere,” he said.

Either chamber of Congress could also consider trying to use its long-dormant “inherent contempt” powers. Such a move would direct the sergeant-at-arms to arrest an official who refused to comply with the directives of Congress.

It would be another escalation in a fight that has been full of them even before it has begun.

Glenn Thrush contributed reporting.

item.title: Here’s the latest.
item.description:
Travelers across the United States and beyond were still facing delays and uncertainty on Saturday as airlines and airports sought to recover from the ground stop the day before that brought air travel to a halt for hours.

Thousands of passengers were stranded on Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered the ground stop. More than 8,200 flights — or over 31 percent of those scheduled for Friday — were canceled nationwide, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm, though some international flights received permission to take off.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said at a news conference on Friday night that the authorities had decided to issue the ground stop after aging air traffic communications equipment became overloaded and began to falter on Friday afternoon.

He said that it would take “some time” for airlines to recover, predicting that flight schedules would return to normal in time for the busy Thanksgiving travel season.

Many who waited at airports until late Friday night had to scramble to find accommodation after their flights were canceled. Some carriers, including United Airlines and American Airlines, began to restore flights after flight traffic was restored on Friday night. Aviation experts have said it could take days to fully restore flight schedules after a halt of this scale.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who appeared alongside Mr. Duffy at the news conference on Friday, said there was no indication that the communications failures had been caused by a cyberattack, though he said that an investigation was underway and that he could not rule out such an attack. He stressed that lives were never in danger.

Mr. Duffy blamed lawmakers for not fully funding upgrades that he said were needed to prevent similar failures. To upgrade aging air traffic facilities and technology, he said, he wanted another $50 billion from the Republican-controlled Congress, which last year approved $12.5 billion for the project.

He said the new amount should be delivered in emergency funding by the end of the year, before control of Congress — and the budget — switches to Democrats.

Here’s what else to know:

If your flight is canceled: You are entitled to a refund if your flight is canceled in the United States, regardless of the reason, or if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and you decide not to take it. Here are other travel tips that might be helpful. Read more ›

Handling the chaos: Radio transmissions between air traffic controllers and pilots at major airports offered a peek at how they navigated the ground stop. Read more ›

Rare halt: Friday’s nationwide ground stop was only the third that the F.A.A. has issued this century. It ranks as the second-longest, after the stop issued in the wake of the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001. There was a shorter one on Jan. 11, 2023, because of an outage in the F.A.A.’s safety-alert system. Read more ›

Democrats’ response: Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House’s top-ranking Democrat, said the stop was “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents” under the Trump administration. He added that Americans deserved timely answers about how and why it happened.
